Ford|Bronco.v: A genuine body-on-frame 4x4, formidable off-road and with successful neo-retro styling. Consumption, motorway noise, rustic build quality and the French malus tax make it an enthusiast's machine.
m: Motorway noise and comfort could be better
Price, malus and rustic build quality
Ford|Bronco.q: Off-road and outdoor enthusiasts prepared to shoulder the running costs
Ford|Bronco.s: Its 288 g/km of CO2 earned it a French malus tax of around €40,000 (2023 scale), on top of the purchase price.
Ford|Bronco.x: Both trims share the 2.7 EcoBoost V6; the Badlands, which sits higher (ground clearance, approach angles) and has locking differentials, is the more capable off-roader.

Ford|Capri.v: The Explorer's coupé-profiled twin, with a bigger boot, well-damped and pleasant to drive. Upper-average consumption, austere interior and a premium over the Explorer count against it.
p: Vast boot, bigger than the Explorer's
Solid range in Extended Range form
m: Real-world consumption on the high side of average
Ford|Capri.q: Drivers wanting a more stylish electric SUV than the Explorer
Ford|Capri.s: Built in Cologne on Volkswagen underpinnings; in early 2026 the Standard Range switched to an LFP battery, more powerful and with more range.
Ford|Capri.x: The Standard Range offers markedly less range; the Extended Range versions go furthest, the rear-wheel-drive 286 hp ahead of the AWD 340 hp, which is quicker but penalised by its second motor.

Ford|Explorer.v: An electric SUV built on Volkswagen underpinnings, practical, long-legged and enjoyable to drive. An average boot, awkward touch controls and hard plastics without the Premium Pack hold it back.
p: Solid range in Extended Range form
m: Average boot, smaller than the ID.4's
Hard plastics without the Premium Pack
Ford|Explorer.q: Families wanting a practical, roomy compact electric SUV
Ford|Explorer.s: Assembled in Cologne on Volkswagen underpinnings; in early 2026 the Standard Range switched to an LFP battery, more powerful and with more range.
Ford|Explorer.x: The rear-wheel-drive Extended Range 286 hp, more agile and with more range, is the one to choose; the quicker AWD 340 hp feels heavier in corners. The Standard Range offers far less range.

Ford|Kuga.v: A roomy family SUV with frugal hybrids and an E85 version that is cheap to run. Facelifted in 2024 with a big screen, it still trails rivals for perceived quality and low-speed comfort.
p: Plug-in hybrid with realistic electric range
m: Hard plastics, perceived quality lags behind
Ford|Kuga.q: Families wanting a comfortable hybrid SUV without paying premium prices
Ford|Kuga.s: The FlexiFuel version runs on E85 bioethanol: it uses more fuel, around 20% more on the motorway, but its cost per kilometre falls markedly.
Ford|Kuga.x: The 180 hp FlexiFuel hybrid cuts running costs on E85; the livelier 243 hp plug-in hybrid suits those who charge often, for a much higher price.

Ford|Mustang.v: One of the last sports cars with a naturally aspirated V8, offered with a manual gearbox and a rare mechanical character. A crushing French malus tax, token rear seats and a very digital cabin temper the enthusiasm.
p: Flexible naturally aspirated V8 with a deep, natural sound
m: Very digital cabin, climate controls on the screen
Ford|Mustang.q: V8 and American-style grand touring enthusiasts
Ford|Mustang.s: In Europe the Mustang now comes only with the 5.0 V8; its French malus tax reached €60,000 in 2024, almost doubling its price.
Ford|Mustang.x: The angrier 453 hp Dark Horse, with a sharper chassis (Torsen differential, standard adaptive dampers), targets enthusiasts; the 446 hp GT pitches a little more. The manual is the most engaging.

Ford|Mustang Mach-E.v: An electric SUV that is comfortable on the road, well insulated and well equipped, with handling that gets a mixed reception across road tests. A modest rear boot, real-world range below the claims and high prices at the top of the range count against it.
p: Front boot as well as the rear boot
m: High prices at the top of the range
Ford|Mustang Mach-E.q: Families wanting a comfortable, well-equipped electric SUV
Ford|Mustang Mach-E.s: Rapid charging peaks at 150 kW, below a Tesla Model Y; the on-board charger accepts 11 kW on AC.
Ford|Mustang Mach-E.x: The RWD Standard Range is enough for most needs; the RWD Extended Range offers the best range; the 487 hp AWD (GT), the quickest and most engaging, comes at a steep price.

Ford|Puma.v: A small SUV that is among the most agile in its class, with a clever boot and a frugal mild hybrid. Narrow rear seats, firm suspension in sporty trim and gearboxes that could be better are its limits.
p: Mild hybrid that fills the turbo lag
m: Rear seats narrower than the 2008 and Captur
Ford|Puma.q: Keen drivers looking for a practical small SUV
Ford|Puma.s: Facelifted in 2024: 12-inch central screen (SYNC 4), digital instruments and the end of the Flexifuel version; only the 1.0 EcoBoost mild hybrid remains.
Ford|Puma.x: The 125 hp is enough and stays frugal; with the six-speed manual, energy recovery causes jerkiness, but Auto Express finds the DCT7 slow. The 170 hp ST version is the liveliest.

Ford|Puma Gen-E.v: The electric version of the Puma keeps its agility and very large boot at a reasonable price. Range remains average, especially on the motorway, which confines it to regional journeys.
p: Very large boot, plus a front boot
m: Rear seats compromised by the battery
Ford|Puma Gen-E.q: Suburban drivers wanting a practical small electric SUV for everyday use
Ford|Puma Gen-E.s: Ford has announced for 2026 a range increase to over 400 km WLTP with the same battery, plus BlueCruise hands-free motorway driving.

Geely|E2.v: A very roomy, well-equipped electric city car for the money, efficient and good at charging. Limited real-world range, modest performance and bland driving make it more of a second car.
p: Generous cabin space, boot and front boot
Comprehensive standard equipment for the price
Low consumption and good charging curve
m: Limited real-world range, especially on the motorway
Everything goes through the screen, irritating driver aids
Geely|E2.q: City dwellers wanting a roomy small EV at a reasonable price
Geely|E2.s: Made in China, it is not eligible for any purchase incentive. Eight-year or 200,000 km warranty; top speed limited to 130 km/h.
Geely|E2.x: The Pro+ (47.1 kWh), the only version tested, is already short on pep and manages around 250 km in mixed use according to L'argus; the less powerful Pro accelerates markedly more slowly and charges more slowly on a rapid charger.

Geely|E5.v: A roomy, comfortable and richly equipped family electric SUV, priced several thousand euros below its European rivals. Bland driving, all-touch ergonomics and average range temper its appeal.
p: Supple suspension, quiet on the motorway
m: Almost all controls on the touchscreen
Geely|E5.q: Families looking for a roomy, well-equipped electric SUV on a tight budget
Geely|E5.s: Sold elsewhere as the EX5. Five Euro NCAP stars. Volvo-derived GEA platform; eight-year or 200,000 km warranty in France.

Geely|Starray EM-i.v: A roomy, comfortable family plug-in hybrid SUV that is very well equipped for the money. Soft handling, an engine that is noisy under hard acceleration and intrusive driver aids stop it standing out.
p: Supple suspension and careful build quality
m: Vague steering and marked body roll in corners
Petrol engine noisy under hard acceleration
Geely|Starray EM-i.q: Families wanting a roomy plug-in hybrid SUV at a low price
Geely|Starray EM-i.s: Five Euro NCAP stars and an eight-year or 200,000 km warranty. Launched in France in spring 2026, where the Geely dealer network is still being built.

Honda|Civic.v: Agile, frugal and roomy, the Civic hybrid impresses with a well-honed e:HEV system and markedly improved build quality. Its high price and near-family-car size are the main criticisms.
p: Cabin space and boot worthy of a family car
Honda|Civic.q: High-mileage drivers wanting a frugal, agile hybrid hatchback
Honda|Civic.s: The 2025 facelift only affects styling and equipment: the hybrid system is unchanged, so road tests of the Civic launched in 2022 still apply.

Honda|HR-V.v: A frugal hybrid SUV that is very smooth in town, well built and versatile thanks to its “Magic Seats”. Rather soft in-gear acceleration, an engine that gets noisy when worked hard and a limited boot temper the verdict.
m: Soft in-gear acceleration, engine noisy uphill
Honda|HR-V.q: Urban or suburban drivers without a charger, looking for a frugal SUV
Honda|HR-V.s: Facelifted in late 2024: discreet styling tweaks, revised centre console and improved sound insulation; the hybrid drivetrain is unchanged.

Honda|Jazz.v: A hybrid city car that is very roomy for its size, frugal and smooth, with unique folding rear seats. Other rivals are more fun to drive and cheaper.
p: Rear space rare for a city car
m: Higher purchase price than many rivals
Honda|Jazz.q: Urban drivers looking for a roomy, frugal city car with no charging
Honda|Jazz.s: Facelifted in 2023: cosmetic tweaks, more hybrid power and a new Advance Sport trim with stiffer suspension.

Honda|Prelude.v: The hybrid Prelude makes a successful return: precise chassis, moderate consumption and a convincing S+ Shift mode. This GT coupé is not very fast, though, and its rear seats and boot are token.
p: S+ Shift mode that livens up the drive
Moderate consumption, even when driven hard
Honda|Prelude.q: Fans of comfortable, frugal coupés who don't need rear seats
Honda|Prelude.s: It uses the Civic's hybrid system. In S+ Shift mode, engine sound is amplified through the speakers. A single, well-equipped trim.

Honda|ZR-V.v: Roomy, well built and frugal in real-world use thanks to a highly polished hybrid system, the ZR-V remains an SUV without much character. Its high price and average boot often make the Civic the better choice.
p: Real-world consumption close to official figures
m: Expensive next to competing hybrid SUVs
Suspension sometimes harsh over small bumps
Honda|ZR-V.q: High-mileage families wanting a frugal hybrid SUV with no charging
Honda|ZR-V.s: It uses the Civic's platform and hybrid system; the Civic has the more practical boot and is cheaper. Four stars in Euro NCAP tests (2023).

Honda|e:Ny1.v: A well-equipped, comfortable small electric SUV, but an expensive one. Modest real-world range, slow rapid charging and a small boot leave it behind more polished rivals.
m: Slow rapid charging for the class
Limited real-world range on the motorway
Honda|e:Ny1.q: Urban or suburban drivers who rarely use the motorway and value equipment
Honda|e:Ny1.s: Derived from the HR-V, it loses the folding “Magic Seats” as the battery takes up the floor. Infotainment judged slow and incomplete.

Hyundai|Bayon.v: A small SUV derived from the i20, roomy, well equipped for the price and with a good warranty, but with no distinctive edge over the Captur, Arona or 2008. Its sole 1.0 petrol engine, without hybrid assistance, lacks punch.
m: 1.0 turbo lacks punch at low revs
Hyundai|Bayon.q: Urban families looking for a simple small SUV with a good warranty
Hyundai|Bayon.s: Hyundai is preparing a heavily reworked Bayon with a new hybrid powertrain, which will closely follow the next i20.
Hyundai|Bayon.x: Road testers prefer the manual gearbox; the DCT-7, slower to respond, blunts already modest performance.

Hyundai|Inster.v: A small EV that is very roomy and versatile for its size, efficient and well equipped. A serious alternative to the R5 and ë-C3, despite basic build quality and less appeal outside town.
Hyundai|Inster.q: City dwellers wanting a compact yet roomy EV
Hyundai|Inster.s: Named World Electric Vehicle of the Year 2025. Five-year unlimited-mileage Hyundai warranty; battery covered for eight years or 160,000 km.
Hyundai|Inster.x: The 49 kWh 115 hp, livelier, with more range and quicker charging, is the most versatile; the cheaper 42 kWh 97 hp offers around 240 km of real-world range according to Top Gear.

Hyundai|Inster Cross.v: The rugged-look version of the Inster: specific bumpers, cladding and wheels, but no all-wheel drive. It keeps the city car's comfort and versatility, but the extra cost buys only a cosmetic gain.
m: Significant extra cost for a cosmetic gain
Hyundai|Inster Cross.q: Inster buyers drawn to the rugged look
Hyundai|Inster Cross.s: Same warranties as the Inster: five years with unlimited mileage, high-voltage battery covered for eight years or 160,000 km.

Hyundai|Ioniq 3.v: An efficient electric hatchback with good range in 61 kWh form and a large boot. Unflattering materials, a low rear seat and its price next to Chinese rivals temper the picture; road tests are divided on how it drives.
p: Low consumption, good range with the 61 kWh
m: Low rear seat, uncomfortable for tall passengers
Hyundai|Ioniq 3.q: Families or commuters wanting a frugal, roomy compact EV
Hyundai|Ioniq 3.s: Assembled in Izmit (Turkey), it qualifies for purchase incentives. Rapid charging peaks at 110 kW, 10-80% in 29 minutes.
Hyundai|Ioniq 3.x: The Battery 42.2 kWh 147 hp, lighter and livelier, is reserved for entry-level trims; the Battery 61 kWh 135 hp, slightly less punchy, brings markedly more range.

Hyundai|Ioniq 5.v: A family electric SUV with distinctive styling, comfortable and renowned for its ultra-fast 800 V charging. The 2024 facelift increased the battery to 84 kWh, but motorway consumption remains high.
Hyundai|Ioniq 5.q: High-mileage families wanting an EV that charges quickly
Hyundai|Ioniq 5.s: Hyundai guarantees the on-board charger (ICCU) of the Ioniq 5 and 6 for 15 years or 300,000 km, and the battery for eight years or 160,000 km.
Hyundai|Ioniq 5.x: The rear-wheel-drive Battery 84 kWh 229 hp, which goes furthest, is the recommended version; the 63 kWh offers markedly less range; the quicker 325 hp 4x4 is only available in N Line trim.

Hyundai|Ioniq 5 N.v: An electric sports car praised for how it drives: simulated N e-Shift gearbox, carefully crafted sound and playful handling. Its weight, range that melts away on track and characterless build quality temper the enthusiasm.
p: Playful handling, oversteers on the throttle
m: Range melts away when driven hard
Characterless build quality for the price
Hyundai|Ioniq 5 N.q: Driving enthusiasts ready to go electric
Hyundai|Ioniq 5 N.s: Its highly configurable driving modes take some learning, and the N Pedal and N e-Shift functions cannot be combined.

Hyundai|Ioniq 6.v: A very aerodynamic electric saloon, among the most efficient on the market, with very fast charging and good refinement. Rear visibility and the boot suffer; in France it is now sold only from stock.
Hyundai|Ioniq 6.q: High-mileage drivers looking for an efficient EV, to snap up from stock
Hyundai|Ioniq 6.s: Hyundai has decided not to sell the facelifted version or the Ioniq 6 N in France: only remaining stock of the original version is still available.

Hyundai|Ioniq 6 N.v: A very fast electric sports saloon, stable and surprisingly engaging thanks to its simulated gearbox. Its weight shows on track, and both rear seats and boot remain compromised.
p: Stable, benign and very fast handling
Hyundai|Ioniq 6 N.q: Driving enthusiasts ready to go electric without giving up the fun
Hyundai|Ioniq 6 N.s: Very wide turning circle, awkward in town; the synthetic sound, which divides opinion, can be switched off.

Hyundai|Ioniq 9.v: A large three-row electric SUV, comfortable, quiet and richly equipped. Its 2.6 tonnes make themselves felt in bends and consumption stays high, but it offers decent value for money.
p: Long range and very fast charging
m: Weight and marked body roll in corners
Swivelling seats usable only when stationary
Hyundai|Ioniq 9.q: Large families looking for a comfortable three-row electric SUV
Hyundai|Ioniq 9.s: High-voltage battery covered for eight years or 160,000 km, on top of Hyundai's five-year unlimited-mileage warranty.
Hyundai|Ioniq 9.x: The rear-wheel-drive Battery 110 kWh 218 hp goes furthest and is the cheapest; the Battery 110 kWh HTRAC 307 hp offers the best compromise; the Battery 110 kWh HTRAC 428 hp, reserved for the top trim, is the quickest.

Hyundai|Kona.v: A small SUV that is now much bigger and roomier, offered as petrol, hybrid and electric. As an EV, the progress is mostly on paper: disappointing real-world range and plastics unworthy of the price.
p: Practical boot, plus a front boot
m: Plastics below what the price demands
Disappointing real-world range as an EV
Hyundai|Kona.q: Buyers torn between hybrid and electric in the same model
Hyundai|Kona.s: The electric Kona benefits from Hyundai's eight-year or 160,000 km battery warranty, on top of the five-year unlimited-mileage cover.
Hyundai|Kona.x: The 1.6 T-GDi Hybrid 138 hp proves frugal, around 5 l/100 km in town, despite a sluggish gearbox; the electric versions disappoint with their real-world range, according to Caradisiac.

Hyundai|Santa Fe.v: A large SUV with boxy, American-inspired styling, very roomy and available with seven seats, with solid build quality. Its 1.6 turbo hybrid sometimes feels stretched for its size and it is expensive.
p: Very generous cabin space and boot
m: Smooth 1.6 engine sometimes stretched for its size
Hyundai|Santa Fe.q: Large families looking for a seven-seat hybrid SUV
Hyundai|Santa Fe.s: Hyundai covers its new cars for five years with unlimited mileage; the hybrid battery is covered for eight years or 160,000 km.
Hyundai|Santa Fe.x: Automobile Propre recommends the smooth, frugal 1.6 T-GDi Hybrid 215 hp for private buyers; the markedly more expensive 1.6 T-GDi Plug-in HTRAC 253 hp is only very economical while its battery is charged.

Hyundai|Tucson.v: A comfortable, roomy family SUV with effective brakes. Its hybrid becomes thirsty as soon as it is pushed, especially on the motorway, and a new generation was unveiled at the 2026 Paris Motor Show.
m: Model nearing the end of its life
Hyundai|Tucson.q: Families who prioritise comfort in a hybrid SUV with a good warranty
Hyundai|Tucson.s: New generation unveiled at the Paris Motor Show (12-18 October 2026): hybrid due in January 2027, plug-in hybrid in summer 2027.

Hyundai|i10.v: A petrol city car that is manoeuvrable, comfortable and well insulated for its size. Its small 1.0, with very long gearing, runs out of breath outside town, and the 2023 facelift came with a sharp price rise.
m: Modest performance from the naturally aspirated 1.0
Sharp price rise at the facelift
Hyundai|i10.q: City dwellers wanting a simple small petrol car with a good warranty
Hyundai|i10.s: Hyundai covers its new cars for five years with unlimited mileage, a warranty that passes to the next owner if the car is sold.
Hyundai|i10.x: The 1.0 Eco 63 hp with the manual gearbox is enough in town; the automated manual gearbox of the 1.0 AMT 63 hp hurts performance and consumption, according to Le Moniteur Automobile.

Hyundai|i20.v: A versatile city car with a generous boot and comprehensive equipment, but less polished than the Clio or Polo, with hard plastics. A new hybrid generation is on the way.
p: Boot among the largest in the class
Hyundai|i20.q: Drivers who put warranty and space ahead of prestige
Hyundai|i20.s: Hyundai has announced a new generation of the i20, followed by the Bayon, with an all-new hybrid powertrain alongside the petrol line-up.

Hyundai|i30.v: A hatchback launched nearly ten years ago, sensible, well built and with a good warranty, on a benign chassis. Its interior has aged next to recent rivals, hence a new facelift is expected.
m: Small 1.0 T-GDi short on in-gear punch
Hyundai|i30.q: Pragmatic drivers attached to a conventional petrol hatchback
Hyundai|i30.s: Facelifted in 2020 and then, discreetly, in 2024, the i30 was due a third facelift in 2026 (front and rear ends, screens). The Fastback has left the range.

Hyundai|i30 SW.v: A compact estate with a large boot, well equipped and comfortable, on a base on sale since 2017. Its small 1.0 three-cylinder lacks torque and its consumption is far from exemplary.
m: Rear seats tight for tall passengers
Hyundai|i30 SW.q: Families looking for a simple, durable petrol estate
Hyundai|i30 SW.s: A third facelift, spotted on the SW, was announced for 2026; it could be the last before the model is replaced.

Jaecoo|5.v: A small SUV that is very well equipped for the price, hushed and frugal as a hybrid. Tuning that could be better (steering, brakes, suspension) and all-touch ergonomics leave it behind European rivals.
p: Hushed cabin, comfortable at low speed
m: Almost all controls on the touchscreen
Artificial steering, tuning could be better
Jaecoo|5.q: Families on a tight budget wanting a well-equipped SUV, hybrid or electric
Jaecoo|5.s: Seven-year or 150,000 km warranty; the electric version's battery is covered for eight years or 160,000 km.
Jaecoo|5.x: The 1.5 SHS-H Hybrid 224 hp is praised for its economy and refinement; the BEV Electric 211 hp offers a bigger boot, but its rapid charging is slow and it is unsettled on the road.

Jaecoo|7.v: A family SUV that is very well equipped for the price, roomy, well built and smooth to drive. A bland chassis, tiresome all-touch ergonomics and high motorway consumption leave it behind the class leaders.
p: Very comprehensive standard equipment for the price
m: All-touch ergonomics tiresome in daily use
Jaecoo|7.q: Families looking for a well-equipped hybrid SUV on a tight budget
Jaecoo|7.s: Seven-year or 150,000 km warranty. Its technical twin, the Chery Tiggo 7, costs around €3,000 less.
Jaecoo|7.x: The 1.5 SHS-H Hybrid 224 hp is frugal in town but thirsty on the motorway; the more expensive 1.5 SHS-P Plug-in Hybrid 279 hp only makes sense if charged very often, and loses boot space.

Jeep|Avenger.v: A stylish small SUV, voted European Car of the Year 2023, offered as an EV and as a hybrid. The 2026 facelift improves build quality up front, but the rear seats remain tight.
m: Tight rear seats, three abreast a struggle
Hard plastics in the back, even after the facelift
Jeep|Avenger.q: City dwellers wanting a small SUV with a rugged look
Jeep|Avenger.s: European Car of the Year 2023. Facelifted in spring 2026: softer materials up front, Matrix LED headlights and a 360° view stitched together from two cameras.
Jeep|Avenger.x: The 1.2 Turbo e-Hybrid 110 hp proves lively and well insulated; the 1.2 Turbo e-Hybrid 4xe 145 hp adds genuine light off-road ability. The Electric 156 hp is technically unchanged by the facelift.

Jeep|Compass.v: Completely renewed on the basis of the Peugeot 3008 and Citroën C5 Aircross, the Compass gains space and goes electric. A slow screen and a personality close to its Stellantis cousins temper the package.
m: Floor not flat with the seats folded
Personality close to other Stellantis models
Jeep|Compass.q: Families looking for a roomy compact SUV, electric or hybrid
Jeep|Compass.s: Built in Italy on the STLA Medium platform of the Peugeot 3008 and Citroën C5 Aircross. A plug-in hybrid, tested by the press in summer 2026, completes the range.

Jeep|Grand Cherokee.v: The Grand Cherokee 4xe shines off-road and is quiet in electric mode. But its price, modest electric range and below-par build quality count against it next to the BMW X5.
p: Calm and quiet in electric mode
m: Expensive next to German premium SUVs
Build quality and body roll behind rivals
Jeep|Grand Cherokee.q: Fans of big American SUVs who occasionally head off the beaten track
Jeep|Grand Cherokee.s: In France it is sold only as a five-seater in Summit Reserve trim; the long seven-seat version is offered in the United States.

Jeep|Wrangler.v: An unrivalled off-roader, the Wrangler 4xe offers a unique character and a few dozen kilometres of electric driving. On the road, vague steering, noise and high consumption make it an enthusiast's vehicle.
p: Good visibility thanks to the boxy shape
m: Vague steering and body roll on the road
High cabin noise on the road
High consumption with the battery empty
Jeep|Wrangler.s: The 2024 model year brought a 12.3-inch touchscreen, a new rear axle and an optional Warn winch integrated into the bumper. Electric range drops in winter.

Kia|EV2.v: A small electric SUV that is comfortable, well insulated and surprisingly roomy for under 4.10 m. With the 42.2 kWh battery, motorway range remains short: the 61 kWh is the one for longer trips.
p: Careful sound insulation for the class
m: Poor motorway range with the 42.2 kWh
Bare entry-level version, price soon climbs
Kia|EV2.q: Urban or suburban drivers with home charging
Kia|EV2.s: Assembled in Žilina (Slovakia), the EV2 is Kia's first car to offer 22 kW AC charging, as an option, compatible with V2L and V2G.
Kia|EV2.x: The livelier Standard Range 42.2 kWh 147 hp is enough in town but barely manages 200 km on the motorway; the Long Range 61 kWh 135 hp is a must for anyone who often uses fast roads.

Kia|EV3.v: A small electric SUV with a generous boot for its size and solid range with the larger battery. Bland driving and no purchase incentive, as it is not built in Europe, weigh on its appeal.
p: Good range with the larger battery
m: Climate-control screen hidden by the steering wheel
No French EV incentive (built in Korea)
Kia|EV3.q: Families wanting a compact, roomy electric SUV
Kia|EV3.s: The heat pump, useful for preserving range in winter, remains an option costing around €1,500.
Kia|EV3.x: The Standard Range 58.3 kWh 204 hp, lighter and cheaper, is enough for many needs; the Long Range 81.4 kWh 204 hp, which also charges faster, is the one for long journeys.

Kia|EV4.v: A long-range electric hatchback, very roomy in the back, comfortable and built in Europe. An average boot, bland driving and prices that soon climb with options are its limits.
m: Average boot and no front boot
Kia|EV4.q: Drivers wanting a long-range electric hatchback rather than an SUV
Kia|EV4.s: Assembled in Žilina (Slovakia) with batteries made in Poland, it qualifies for French purchase incentives, unlike the Korean-built EV3.

Kia|EV4 Fastback.v: The four-door version of the EV4, more aerodynamic and with a larger boot. A rare alternative to SUVs, with top-tier range but reduced rear visibility.
p: Range among the best on the market
Bigger boot than the five-door EV4
m: Divisive styling, especially at the rear
Kia|EV4 Fastback.q: High-mileage drivers who prefer an electric saloon to an SUV
Kia|EV4 Fastback.s: A four-door saloon built in South Korea, unlike the five-door EV4 assembled in Slovakia: check its eligibility for incentives.

Kia|EV4 GT.v: A lively all-wheel-drive electric hatchback, comfortable day to day and fun thanks to its virtual gearbox. Its price, well above the Cupra Born VZ and ID.3 GTI, and its average range count against it.
p: Good balance of comfort and dynamism
m: Very high price next to sporty rivals
Small boot and no front storage
Only average range and rapid charging
Kia|EV4 GT.q: Hot hatch fans prepared to pay a lot for a fun EV
Kia|EV4 GT.s: Built in Slovakia with a seven-year or 150,000 km warranty. The heat pump and the 22 kW bidirectional on-board charger remain optional.

Kia|EV5.v: A comfortable, quiet and very roomy family electric SUV. Average rapid charging, bland handling and overly chatty warnings stop it dominating the class.
p: Comfortable and quiet on the motorway
m: Climate-control screen hidden by the steering wheel
Kia|EV5.q: Families looking for a roomy, comfortable electric SUV for long trips
Kia|EV5.s: 400 V architecture: the claimed 10-80% in 30 minutes is achieved only with a preconditioned battery, according to electrive.
Kia|EV5.x: Only the 2WD 217 hp has actually been tested: adequate performance, limited traction when pushed. The 4WD 265 hp accelerates harder and can tow more.

Kia|EV6.v: An electric SUV with ultra-fast charging, long range and benign handling, improved by the 2024 facelift. Rather firm suspension, limited rear headroom and touch controls are the downsides.
m: Rear headroom limited by the roofline
Kia|EV6.q: High-mileage drivers wanting an EV that charges quickly on the motorway
Kia|EV6.s: Facelifted in 2024: battery increased to 84 kWh, maximum charging power of 258 kW, revised screens and infotainment.
Kia|EV6.x: The twin-motor Long Range 84 kWh 325 hp is markedly quicker and has better traction than the 229 hp; it is the version preferred by Le Guide de l'auto.

Kia|EV6 GT.v: The 650 hp version of the EV6, very fast, quick to charge and well damped. Less playful than the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, it remains short on thrills and its artificial sound is unconvincing.
Kia|EV6 GT.q: Enthusiasts wanting a very high-performance EV for every day
Kia|EV6 GT.s: Renewed in 2025, it shares the 84 kWh battery and 650 hp of the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, with a more discreet character.

Kia|EV9.v: A large seven-seat electric SUV, roomy, comfortable and very well equipped. Imposing size, undynamic driving and high prices are the trade-offs.
p: Comfortable suspension, even in the back
m: High prices at the top of the range
Kia|EV9.q: Large families wanting seven proper seats in an EV
Kia|EV9.s: Its driver aids, judged intrusive, have to be switched off every time the car is started. Rivals: Mercedes EQE SUV and Volvo EX90.

Kia|EV9 GT.v: The 508 hp version of the EV9, which keeps seven seats and genuine comfort. Surprisingly agile for its size thanks to its adaptive suspension, it is very expensive for a Kia.
p: Strong performance for a 5 m SUV
m: Weight makes itself felt in tight corners
Kia|EV9 GT.q: Large families wanting seven seats and sports-car performance
Kia|EV9 GT.s: Available to order in France since July 2025, it gets road-scanning adaptive suspension and a torque-vectoring electronic differential.

Kia|Niro.v: A roomy compact hybrid SUV, pleasant day to day and with a seven-year warranty. The press is divided on its economy, and the 2026 facelift keeps only the conventional hybrid, with no plug-in or electric version.
m: Modest performance, engine noisy when accelerating
Kia|Niro.q: Drivers wanting an economical hybrid SUV with no charging hassle
Kia|Niro.s: Facelifted and available to order since summer 2026 as a hybrid only: the electric and plug-in hybrid versions have left the French range.

Kia|Picanto.v: A very manoeuvrable city car, with one of the largest boots in its class and an updated look. An engine that struggles outside town, narrow rear seats and a dated platform limit it.
p: Ideal manoeuvrability and size in town
One of the largest boots in the class
m: Rear seats best suited to children
Kia|Picanto.q: City dwellers wanting a simple, manoeuvrable small car
Kia|Picanto.s: Facelifted for the second time in 2024, the third generation dates from 2017. No hybrid or electric version is offered.

Kia|Seltos.v: A well-thought-out compact hybrid SUV, roomier than its predecessor, with a large boot and clear ergonomics. Soft suspension, marked body roll and a price above its rivals temper its appeal.
Kia|Seltos.q: Families looking for a roomy compact hybrid SUV with no charging
Kia|Seltos.s: New to Europe, it shares its platform with the Niro; the first generation, launched in 2019, was not sold here.

Kia|Sorento.v: A large seven-seat SUV, roomy and very comfortable on the road. As a plug-in hybrid, its modest real-world electric range and slow charging leave it behind the best rivals.
p: Seven seats and a spacious cabin
m: Slow charging and small fuel tank
Kia|Sorento.q: Large families wanting seven seats who travel a lot
Kia|Sorento.s: Facelifted in 2024 (revised front end and on-board tech), it has never been so expensive, while remaining cheaper than the electric EV9.

Kia|Sportage.v: A roomy, comfortable and well-built family SUV with a seven-year warranty. The facelift brings it closer to premium, prices included, and its touch controls remain awkward.
Kia|Sportage.q: Families looking for a versatile compact SUV with a good warranty
Kia|Sportage.s: Facelifted in late 2025: “Constellation” lighting signature, 10-inch head-up display. In France the range is limited to the 239 hp hybrid, with no plug-in.

Kia|Stonic.v: Launched in 2017 and substantially facelifted in late 2025, the Stonic gains a big screen and a revised front end, but no full hybrid. Simple and economical, it remains less practical and less comfortable than its recent rivals.
p: Comprehensive driver aids for the class
m: Old platform, less practical than rivals
Kia|Stonic.q: Urban drivers wanting a simple, economical small SUV
Kia|Stonic.s: Facelifted in late 2025 (25 mm longer, boot unchanged), it keeps Kia's seven-year warranty, one of its main strengths.
Kia|Stonic.x: The 100 hp and 115 hp mild-hybrid 1.0 T-GDi engines offer similar, adequate performance; the smooth DCT7 gearbox is slow to shift down, while the six-speed manual is judged pleasant.

Lancia|Gamma.v: An SUV with distinctive styling and ambience that favours comfort and quietness over sportiness; its shared underpinnings and price, however, struggle to set it apart from rivals.
p: Comfortable suspension and good sound insulation
Lots of rear legroom, vast boot
m: Heavy EVs, more comfortable than sporty
Rapid charging merely adequate, high price
Lancia|Gamma.q: Families looking for a comfortable SUV with distinctive styling
Lancia|Gamma.s: It shares its platform, batteries, wheelbase, boot and Melfi factory with the DS N°7, which is positioned higher on price.
Lancia|Gamma.x: The much lighter 1.2 Ibrida 145 hp is livelier in corners but short on acceleration; the HF Integrale 350 hp is fast without being sporty; the Elettrica 245 hp is aimed mainly at range.

Lancia|Ypsilon.v: A city car with original styling and ambience, well equipped, but very close to a Peugeot 208, whose cramped rear seats it keeps. An honest proposition rather than a premium benchmark.
Lancia|Ypsilon.q: City dwellers drawn to Italian style, mostly driving alone or as a couple
Lancia|Ypsilon.s: It shares its platform and engines with the Peugeot 208; the electric HF uses the mechanicals of the Alfa Romeo Junior Veloce.
Lancia|Ypsilon.x: The 1.2 Ibrida 100 hp is judged frugal and responsive, despite slight jerkiness in town. The Elettrica HF 280 hp is lively and comfortable but falls short on traction, braking and price.

Land Rover|Range Rover.v: Regal comfort, a beautifully finished cabin and undiminished off-road ability: the Range Rover remains the benchmark luxury SUV and improves on the road. But it is very heavy, and its price confines it to a select clientele.
p: Luxurious cabin with a clean, careful design
m: Very high price and French malus tax
Fewer physical buttons since the 2024 update
Land Rover|Range Rover.q: Wealthy buyers wanting a comfortable luxury SUV that is capable off-road
Land Rover|Range Rover.s: Updated in 2024 (large touchscreen). The long wheelbase offers limousine-like space in the back, but its seats fold less flat.
Land Rover|Range Rover.x: The very refined 3.0 D350 350 hp diesel is Autocar's favourite engine. The smooth, punchy 3.0 P460e 460 hp and 3.0 P550e 550 hp plug-in hybrids are judged the most recommendable by Top Gear, but their real-world electric range falls short of the claims.

Land Rover|Range Rover Evoque.v: The facelifted baby Range Rover still appeals with its styling and comfort, but it remains less practical and more expensive than its German rivals, with lacklustre handling.
p: Good ride comfort and careful sound insulation
m: Limited rear seats, boot and visibility
Expensive next to the BMW X1 and Mercedes GLA
Climate controls relegated to the touchscreen
Land Rover|Range Rover Evoque.q: Buyers who put style and comfort ahead of interior space
Land Rover|Range Rover Evoque.s: The 2023 facelift replaces the two screens and rotary controls with a single 11.4-inch touchscreen, which also handles the climate control.
Land Rover|Range Rover Evoque.x: The 2.0 D200 204 hp diesel is the recommended version, powerful and frugal (7.5 l/100 km recorded in winter). The 1.5 P270e 269 hp plug-in hybrid delivers its electric range but is thirsty with the battery empty.

Land Rover|Range Rover Sport.v: The Sport offers the comfort and quietness of the full-size Range Rover with sharper handling. The press ranks it among the most polished luxury SUVs, without judging it dominant, and points to its price.
m: Very high price and running costs
Bulky size in town and on narrow roads
Almost all controls relegated to the screen
Land Rover|Range Rover Sport.q: Wealthy buyers wanting a comfortable, fast luxury SUV that can go off-road
Land Rover|Range Rover Sport.s: The press recommends the Stormer pack (rear-wheel steering, active anti-roll) for the best handling, and 21- or 22-inch wheels rather than 23s.
Land Rover|Range Rover Sport.x: The 3.0 D350 350 hp diesel is judged ideal: smooth, frugal and with a long range. The 3.0 P460e 460 hp runs out of breath with the battery empty, which the 3.0 P550e 550 hp fixes. The 4.4 P540 537 hp V8 is a delight but very thirsty.

Land Rover|Range Rover Velar.v: Facelifted, the Velar gains a better screen and remains a refined, comfortable SUV. But it is expensive, not much fun to drive and squeezed between the Evoque and the Range Rover Sport.
p: Elegant styling that has aged well
High levels of comfort and refinement
m: Physical controls removed, ergonomics a step back
Rear seat comfortable for only two
Land Rover|Range Rover Velar.q: Buyers who care more about design and comfort than driving pleasure
Land Rover|Range Rover Velar.s: Road tests of the 2.0 P400e 404 hp hybrid record 50-60 km of real-world electric range; with the battery empty, its four-cylinder becomes noisy and thirsty.

Leapmotor|B03X.v: A very roomy, efficient small electric SUV that is well equipped for the price, but whose vague handling and all-touch ergonomics betray unfinished development.
p: Remarkable boot and versatility for its size
m: Vague steering, body roll and traction could be better
Almost all controls on the touchscreen
Leapmotor|B03X.q: Urban families looking for a practical, affordable small electric SUV
Leapmotor|B03X.s: Leapmotor promises software updates to fix the handling and driver aids; the chassis has not had the European tuning given to the B05.
Leapmotor|B03X.x: The Pro Max 53 kWh 197 hp, the only version tested, is clearly the one to choose: livelier, with more range and quicker charging than the Pro 39.8 kWh 177 hp.

Leapmotor|B05.v: A well-equipped electric hatchback that charges quickly and is markedly cheaper than its European rivals; a small boot, steering that lacks weight and intrusive driver aids count against it.
m: Small boot, no front or underfloor storage
Intrusive driver aids and all-touch controls
Leapmotor|B05.q: Couples or small families wanting an electric hatchback at a reasonable price
Leapmotor|B05.s: Its chassis was tuned by Stellantis engineers, with a different set-up from the Chinese version (Lafa 5).
Leapmotor|B05.x: The Pro Max 67.1 kWh 218 hp, the most widely tested, offers range judged worthwhile and more powerful charging than the Pro 56.2 kWh 218 hp; no road test compares how they drive.

Leapmotor|B10.v: A roomy, comfortable and well-equipped compact electric SUV at a keen price, but vague steering, average range and an all-touch interface limit its appeal.
p: Generous cabin space, especially in the back
Plentiful standard equipment for the price
m: Light, vague steering, marked body roll
Almost all controls on the touchscreen
Leapmotor|B10.q: Budget-conscious families driving mostly in and around town
Leapmotor|B10.s: The lane-keeping aids trigger wrongly; an over-the-air update is due to add one-pedal driving.
Leapmotor|B10.x: The Pro Max 67.1 kWh 218 hp brings more range and more powerful rapid charging than the Pro 56.2 kWh 218 hp, whose range is judged short for a family car.

Leapmotor|C10.v: A very roomy family SUV that is well equipped for the price, comfortable but no fun to drive, let down by intrusive driver aids and, as an EV, by slow charging.
p: Very comprehensive standard equipment for the price
Careful build quality, responsive central screen
m: Rather small boot for the class
Slow rapid charging on the electric version
Leapmotor|C10.q: Families who put space and equipment ahead of driving pleasure
Leapmotor|C10.s: Sold in France through the dealer network of Stellantis, Leapmotor's partner; chassis retuned for Europe, over-the-air updates promised for the driver aids.
Leapmotor|C10.x: The 1.5 E-Hybrid 220 hp (range extender) is reassuring on long trips but loses boot space and punch with the battery empty; the electric Pro 69.9 kWh is simpler but charges slowly.

Leapmotor|T03.v: A small, well-equipped electric city car that is easy to live with in town, but imprecise handling outside built-up areas, basic build quality and modest range limit its use.
p: Generous standard equipment for the price
Very manoeuvrable in town, light steering
Decent rear space for its size
m: Hard plastics and basic build quality
Range and rapid charging marginal outside town
Leapmotor|T03.q: City dwellers looking for a well-equipped small EV for town
Leapmotor|T03.s: Only four seats; the touchscreen, which also runs the climate control, offers neither Apple CarPlay nor Android Auto.

Lexus|ES.v: The eighth-generation Lexus executive saloon, offered as a hybrid or an EV. Comfort, quietness and rear space are its strengths, but it is less dynamic than its German rivals and its boot is impractical.
m: Less dynamic than its German rivals
Hybrid's CVT noisy under hard acceleration
Lexus|ES.q: High-mileage drivers or demanding rear passengers who put comfort first
Lexus|ES.s: Warranty extendable up to 10 years if the car is serviced within the Lexus network. The EV charges from 10-80% in about 28 minutes.
Lexus|ES.x: The 350e 224 hp, the most tested, is judged quiet and brisk enough. The hybrid has only been tested as the 350h, more powerful than the 300h sold here: frugal, but its CVT gets noisy under heavy load.

Lexus|LBX.v: A small premium SUV derived from the Toyota Yaris Cross: frugal, agile and well presented. Its cramped rear seats and high price for its size count against it next to the Audi Q2 or DS 3.
p: Neat presentation, despite hard plastics lower down
m: Unintuitive touch controls on the steering wheel
Lexus|LBX.q: City dwellers or couples wanting a small premium hybrid
Lexus|LBX.s: Lexus Relax programme: warranty extended up to 10 years if annual servicing is done within the network.

Lexus|NX.v: A premium hybrid SUV that is frugal around town, quiet and well built: a rare non-plug-in alternative to the Audi Q5 and BMW X3. The touchscreen is unintuitive and the engine makes itself heard under hard acceleration.
p: Frugal hybrid in town, no charging needed
m: Engine revs hard under heavy load
Lexus|NX.q: Executives or families looking for a frugal premium hybrid SUV
Lexus|NX.s: A facelifted NX (next-generation hybrids, revised dashboard) was revealed in September 2026, for a global launch at the end of 2026; no European date has been given.
Lexus|NX.x: The 2.5 350h Hybrid 200 hp suits private buyers without a charger. The 450h+ 4WD, much quicker and able to cover around 60 km on electric power, is aimed mainly at fleets for its tax treatment.

Lexus|RX.v: A large premium plug-in hybrid SUV: quiet, spacious and very well finished. Irritating touch controls, modest electric range and less power than its German rivals, all for a high price.
p: Reasonable consumption with a flat battery
m: Unintuitive touch controls on the steering wheel
CVT gearbox noisy under hard acceleration
Less powerful than its German rivals
Lexus|RX.q: Executives or well-off families wanting a relaxing premium SUV
Lexus|RX.s: Warranty of 3 years/100,000 km, with the battery covered for 8 years/160,000 km; the Lexus Relax programme extends it if servicing is done within the network.

Lexus|RZ.v: A premium electric SUV facelifted in 2025: quiet, very well finished and with more range than before. Efficiency is still average, range on the all-wheel-drive versions is modest, and the 550e F Sport is expensive.
m: Average efficiency, modest range with all-wheel drive
High price in F Sport trim
Lexus|RZ.q: Fans of Japanese premium cars making the switch to electric
Lexus|RZ.s: Facelifted in 2025: 77 kWh battery, 22 kW AC charging and, on the 550e F Sport, a “yoke” steering wheel and a simulated eight-speed gearbox.
Lexus|RZ.x: The 350e, whose performance is judged adequate, has the longest range. The 550e, the only one to get the “yoke” wheel (precise according to L'argus, disconcerting according to coches.com), is the most expensive and has the shortest range.

Lexus|UX.v: A comfortable, well-insulated premium compact SUV that is very frugal around town. Against the BMW X1 or Audi Q3, it falls short on rear space and a cabin that has aged.
Lexus|UX.q: Urban drivers or executives wanting a frugal premium SUV
Lexus|UX.s: Lexus Relax programme: warranty extended up to 10 years if annual servicing is done within the network.

MG|3.v: The cheapest hybrid city car on the market and one of the most powerful, it is frugal and well equipped. A drab interior, hard plastics and touch controls leave it trailing a Clio E-Tech, which is nicer to drive.
p: Very low starting price for a hybrid
m: Air conditioning controlled via the touchscreen
MG|3.q: Buyers on a tight budget seeking a well-equipped new hybrid
MG|3.s: MG 7-year warranty, capped at 150,000 km. L'argus recommends the Comfort trim, better equipped for everyday use and for resale.

MG|4.v: Facelifted, the MG4 gains a more modern dashboard, physical controls and better sound insulation, without losing its rear-wheel-drive appeal. Rear space and boot remain limited.
m: Heavier LFP battery, less punchy in-gear acceleration
MG|4.q: Drivers wanting an enjoyable electric hatchback at the best price
MG|4.s: March 2026 facelift: the 51 kWh is dropped, the 64 kWh switches to LFP and the 77 kWh returns. The 435 hp XPower carries over unchanged.
MG|4.x: The 64 kWh 190 hp, now with LFP chemistry, is adequate but pulls less eagerly than before; the 77 kWh 245 hp offers more range. The 64 kWh AWD XPOWER 435 hp, firmer and no more agile, only makes sense on slippery roads.

MG|4 EV Urban.v: A simpler, cheaper version of the MG4, on a different, front-wheel-drive platform. Roomy, frugal and very keenly priced, it is more ordinary to drive and slow to charge with the small battery.
m: Rear suspension skittish on poor roads
Slow charging on the small battery
MG|4 EV Urban.q: Buyers wanting a roomy electric hatchback at the lowest price
MG|4 EV Urban.s: Despite its name, it has nothing in common with the MG4: E3 platform, front-wheel drive and a torsion-beam rear axle. MG 7-year/150,000 km warranty.
MG|4 EV Urban.x: The 54 kWh 160 hp, the most tested, proves frugal and often exceeds 400 km. On the cheaper 43 kWh, Le Moniteur Automobile judges range and rapid charging to lag behind rivals.

MG|Cyberster.v: An electric roadster with polished styling and strong performance, more grand tourer than sports car. Its weight tells on twisty roads and its multi-screen ergonomics are confusing.
MG|Cyberster.q: Electric convertible fans who prefer relaxed cruising
MG|Cyberster.s: MG manufacturer warranty of 7 years or 150,000 km. Its powered scissor doors take a few seconds to operate.
MG|Cyberster.x: The 4WD 510 hp is the most tested version. The 2WD 340 hp, judged satisfactory by Le Moniteur Automobile, nonetheless lacks punch next to the 4WD, for a modest price difference.

MG|EHS.v: A large family SUV offered as a full hybrid or plug-in hybrid, generous in space and equipment for its price, with careful build quality. Touchscreen-centred ergonomics and uninspiring handling count against it.
MG|EHS.q: Families wanting a large electrified SUV without a premium budget
MG|EHS.s: Sold as the MG HS outside France, notably in Belgium. MG 7-year/150,000 km warranty.
MG|EHS.x: The lighter 1.5 Turbo Hybrid+ 224 hp is livelier and frugal without a charger. The 1.5 Turbo PHEV 272 hp covers around 80 km on electric power but charges slowly, with no rapid charging, and feels less powerful than claimed.

MG|IM5.v: A large electric saloon that is very fast, quiet and well equipped for its price, and at ease on long journeys; numb steering, all-screen ergonomics and poor rear visibility keep it out of premium territory.
p: Comfort and quietness at motorway speeds
Very comprehensive equipment, powerful rapid charging
MG|IM5.q: High-mileage drivers seeking a fast, well-equipped electric saloon
MG|IM5.s: It wears only the IM logo, with no MG badge; the 4WD adds four-wheel steering, which makes manoeuvring in town easier.
MG|IM5.x: The 407 hp 2WD, already very fast, offers the best range and seems the most coherent choice; the 751 hp 4WD gains traction and stability, but its performance is of little use and it consumes more.

MG|IM6.v: A fast, spacious large electric SUV, very well equipped for its price and with some of the quickest charging around; yet it lacks character, is heavy and leaves too many controls to the screens.
m: Too many controls relegated to screens
MG|IM6.q: High-mileage families seeking a fast-charging electric SUV
MG|IM6.s: Only the 4WD gets adaptive air suspension; four-wheel steering makes this large SUV more manoeuvrable in town.
MG|IM6.x: The 407 hp 2WD is judged the most sensible choice; the 751 hp 4WD adds air suspension that smooths out the road well, but its extra performance counts for little day to day.

MG|MGS5 EV.v: Successor to the ZS EV, this electric SUV makes clear progress in build quality and efficiency. Formidable value for money in equipment terms against the Kia EV3 or Skoda Elroq, but motorway range is tight.
MG|MGS5 EV.q: Suburban drivers seeking a well-equipped electric SUV
MG|MGS5 EV.s: It replaces the MG ZS EV. MG manufacturer warranty of 7 years or 150,000 km, battery included.
MG|MGS5 EV.x: Only the 64 kWh 231 hp has been tested: frugal and lively, it should account for most sales. The cheaper 49 kWh 170 hp makes do with slower AC charging and has no heat pump.

MG|MGS6 EV.v: A spacious large electric family SUV, well finished and well equipped for its price, but its real-world range, average charging and comfort that could be better leave it behind the best rivals.
p: Lots of space, especially in the rear
Comprehensive standard equipment for the price
m: Average real-world range and rapid charging
MG|MGS6 EV.q: Families seeking a roomy large electric SUV at a reasonable price
MG|MGS6 EV.s: It debuts an augmented-reality head-up display at MG; a front boot (frunk) supplements the main boot, which is smaller on the Dual Motor version.
MG|MGS6 EV.x: The lighter 77 kWh 244 hp is judged more pleasant, more comfortable and longer-legged; the very fast 77 kWh Dual Motor 361 hp gets unsettled on poor surfaces and is not worth the extra cost.

MG|ZS.v: A hybrid small SUV offering very strong value in price, equipment and warranty, roomy and with comfortable seats. An unrefined hybrid system, average handling and heavy fuel use on the motorway leave it behind the class leaders.
p: One of the cheapest hybrids in its segment
m: Slow in-gear acceleration, gearbox slow to kick down
Infotainment could be better, dated mapping
MG|ZS.q: Families seeking a roomy hybrid SUV on a budget
MG|ZS.s: It shares its hybrid powertrain with the MG3. Manufacturer warranty of 7 years or 150,000 km.

Mazda|2.v: Derived from the Toyota Yaris Hybrid, it borrows its renowned hybrid system and great frugality in town. Its 6-year warranty doesn't make up for a drab cabin and prices above those of the Clio E-Tech and 208 Hybrid.
Mazda|2.q: City drivers seeking a frugal, reliable hybrid
Mazda|2.s: It is a rebadged Toyota Yaris Hybrid built in France. Its 6-year/150,000 km warranty falls short of the Yaris's, which runs up to 10 years at Toyota.

Mazda|3.v: A hatchback with polished design and very high-quality finish, enjoyable to drive with its naturally aspirated 2.5. Rear space, boot and rear visibility lag behind the Golf or 308.
Mazda|3.q: Drivers who value design and build quality
Mazda|3.s: The 140 hp naturally aspirated 2.5 has replaced the 122 hp 2.0. Mazda 6-year/150,000 km warranty.
Mazda|3.x: The 2.5 E-Skyactiv-G 140 hp is adequate, to the point of making the 186 hp Skyactiv-X dispensable according to one test. Its manual gearbox is praised; the smooth automatic lacks responsiveness.

Mazda|3 Berline.v: The three-box saloon version of the Mazda 3 shares its careful finish and the appeal of the naturally aspirated 2.5, with a much bigger boot than the hatchback. Limited rear space and firm damping remain its weak points.
Mazda|3 Berline.q: Fans of a classic compact, well-finished saloon
Mazda|3 Berline.s: The 140 hp naturally aspirated 2.5 has replaced the 122 hp 2.0. Mazda 6-year/150,000 km warranty.
Mazda|3 Berline.x: The 2.5 E-Skyactiv-G 140 hp is a clear step up on the old 2.0, especially with the automatic gearbox; the 2.0 E-Skyactiv-X 186 hp is only slightly quicker. No version makes it a sports car.

Mazda|6e.v: A large electric saloon of Changan origin: elegant, spacious and well equipped for its price. Unconvincing dynamic tuning, laborious all-touch ergonomics and a modest boot.
m: Slow charging with the larger battery
Mazda|6e.q: Regular drivers wanting a spacious, well-equipped large electric saloon
Mazda|6e.s: Built on Changan's EPA1 platform, shared with the Deepal SL03, it is produced in China, where it is sold as the EZ-6.
Mazda|6e.x: The entry-level Electric 258 hp is the most recommended: its LFP battery charges from 10-80% in 24 min. The Electric Long Range 258 hp gains 73 km but, capped at 90 kW, needs 47 min.

Mazda|CX-30.v: A compact SUV with polished styling, good build quality and precise handling, well equipped for its price. Limited rear space, firm suspension in town and a sluggish entry-level 2.5 count against it.
Mazda|CX-30.q: Drivers demanding on build quality and driving pleasure
Mazda|CX-30.s: The 140 hp 2.5 has replaced the old 2.0; all-wheel drive is reserved for the Skyactiv-X. Mazda 6-year/150,000 km warranty.
Mazda|CX-30.x: The 2.5 e-Skyactiv-G 140 hp, judged adequate by some, needs to be worked hard; the 2.0 e-Skyactiv-X 186 hp is quicker and more frugal. The manual gearbox is preferred to the automatic, judged hesitant.

Mazda|CX-60.v: A family SUV with a frugal six-cylinder diesel and a flattering finish. The 2025 chassis tweaks make the ride less harsh, without turning it into a benchmark for smoothness.
m: Suspension still firm on poor roads
Mazda|CX-60.q: High-mileage drivers seeking a well-finished large diesel SUV
Mazda|CX-60.s: Criticised for its ride at launch, it received revised suspension in 2025 (rear anti-roll bar removed, softer rear springs).
Mazda|CX-60.x: The 3.3 e-Skyactiv-D diesel is the most pleasant, and the livelier 254 hp justifies its premium over the 200 hp. The 2.5 e-Skyactiv PHEV 327 hp is noisy when revved, with sometimes abrupt transitions.

Mazda|CX-6e.v: An electric SUV with polished styling, good sound insulation and lots of rear space. Its huge, unintuitive central screen and merely average range and charging leave it behind the best.
m: Modest boot for a family SUV
Mazda|CX-6e.q: Families wanting a roomy electric SUV without chasing record range
Mazda|CX-6e.s: Designed on a Changan base and built in China, it has no eco-score and therefore no French EV incentive. Warranty of 6 years/150,000 km, battery 8 years/160,000 km.

Mazda|CX-80.v: The stretched seven-seat version of the CX-60, frugal and pleasant with the six-cylinder diesel, and more comfortable than its sibling. The plug-in hybrid, noisy with a flat battery, is less convincing.
Mazda|CX-80.q: Large families seeking a well-finished seven-seat SUV
Mazda|CX-80.s: Both powertrains can tow a 2,500 kg braked trailer. Mazda 6-year/150,000 km warranty.
Mazda|CX-80.x: The 3.3 e-Skyactiv-D 254 hp is the testers' choice: smooth, frugal and refined. The 2.5 e-Skyactiv PHEV 327 hp, cheaper and more tax-efficient, proves noisy and hesitant with a flat battery.

Mazda|MX-30.v: An unconventional SUV with a rotary range extender, rear-hinged doors and original materials. A singular proposition, but impractical, and withdrawn from the European line-up in early 2026.
m: Awkward access to the rear seats
High consumption once the rotary kicks in
Model at the end of its life
Mazda|MX-30.q: Tech enthusiasts who drive mostly on electric power
Mazda|MX-30.s: Mazda stopped selling the MX-30 R-EV in Europe in early 2026 because of poor sales: availability is limited to existing stock.

Mazda|MX-5.v: The benchmark affordable roadster: light, precise and delightfully simple mechanically, with no direct rival. A cramped cabin, almost no storage and modest power are the flip side.
p: Manual soft top quick to operate
Mazda|MX-5.q: Purist drivers seeking an affordable convertible
Mazda|MX-5.s: Facelifted in 2024 (8.8-inch screen, more driver aids), it has lost its 184 hp 2.0, withdrawn because of emissions standards.

Mazda|MX-5 RF.v: The MX-5 with a retractable hard top keeps the roadster's driving appeal, and its fastback profile is attractive. Wind noise with the roof open, a cabin with no storage and a premium over the soft top are the price to pay.
m: Buffeting and wind noise with the roof open
Extra cost and weight over the soft top
Mazda|MX-5 RF.q: Roadster fans who drive all year round
Mazda|MX-5 RF.s: Facelifted in 2024: 8.8-inch screen, recalibrated steering and driver aids required by the GSR 2 regulation, judged intrusive. Mazda 6-year/150,000 km warranty.

Mercedes-Benz|AMG GT.v: Bigger, more comfortable and now all-wheel drive (except the GT 43), the second-generation AMG GT becomes a highly capable 2+2 GT. The press praises its V8 and handling, but finds it less communicative than a Porsche 911.
p: Much improved comfort and build quality
m: Very high price and French malus tax
Mercedes-Benz|AMG GT.q: Fans of powerful coupés wanting a 2+2 GT usable every day
Mercedes-Benz|AMG GT.s: Second generation (C192) launched at the end of 2023: a 4.73 m 2+2 hatchback coupé with a 321 l boot (192 l for the plug-in hybrid). The rear seats are only suitable for young children.
Mercedes-Benz|AMG GT.x: The “4.0 63 4MATIC+ 585 hp” is the most tested and most recommended, with Caradisiac preferring it to the “4.0 63 S E Performance 816 hp”, which is faster but heavier and more expensive. The “2.0 43 421 hp”, the only rear-wheel-drive version, lacks character and responsiveness according to evo; the “4.0 63 Pro 4MATIC+ 612 hp” has only been assessed by L'argus, on a soaking-wet circuit.

Mercedes-Benz|AMG GT 4 Portes.v: The first all-electric AMG, the GT 4-Door wins over the press with its precise steering, cohesive chassis and convincing V8 simulation. It remains heavy and expensive, and its interior styling divides opinion.
Mercedes-Benz|AMG GT 4 Portes.q: Keen drivers ready to go electric without giving up the thrills
Mercedes-Benz|AMG GT 4 Portes.s: Revealed in May 2026, it debuts AMG's 800 V electric platform, with charging claimed at up to 600 kW (10-80% in 11 min) but only 11 kW on AC. Sales are due to start in March 2027.
Mercedes-Benz|AMG GT 4 Portes.x: The press drove the “GT 55 816 hp” on the road and the “GT 63 1169 hp” at the Ascari circuit; the “GT 53 544 hp”, which has the longest range, has not yet been tested. The GT 63 adds a Boost function lasting around one minute and the AMG Race Engineer assistant, but Top Gear names the GT 55 as the version to go for.

Mercedes-Benz|CLA.v: Crowned 2026 European Car of the Year, the electric CLA shines for its efficiency and rapid charging; the 48 V hybrid proves pleasant and frugal. Low rear seats, patchy plastics and high prices.
p: Very low consumption as an EV
Good balance of comfort and dynamism
m: High prices, hybrid priced like the EV
Mercedes-Benz|CLA.q: High-mileage drivers wanting a frugal premium saloon for long trips
Mercedes-Benz|CLA.s: Named 2026 European Car of the Year, a first for Mercedes since 1974. 400 V rapid chargers require a converter, available as an option.
Mercedes-Benz|CLA.x: The CLA 250+ EQ is preferred to the electric CLA 200, which has less range and is slower to charge on long trips. The 1.5 CLA 220 hybrid, pleasant and free of range worries, costs more.

Mercedes-Benz|CLA Shooting Brake.v: Mercedes' first electric estate, the CLA Shooting Brake appeals with its range, rapid charging and refinement. Boot and rear space remain limited for an estate, and the price is high.
p: Long range, rapid charging with the 85 kWh battery
Quiet and comfortable at a steady cruise
Mercedes-Benz|CLA Shooting Brake.q: Drivers who put range and style before load space
Mercedes-Benz|CLA Shooting Brake.s: With the 85 kWh battery, a 10-80% charge takes around twenty minutes; a 101 l front boot (frunk) adds to the 455 l boot. Charging at 400 V chargers is optional.
Mercedes-Benz|CLA Shooting Brake.x: The CLA 250+ EQ is the recommended version, for its range and performance. The very fast CLA 350 EQ 4MATIC costs more for less range; the CLA 200 and the hybrids have not been tested.

Mercedes-Benz|CLE.v: An elegant large coupé that replaces the C-Class and E-Class coupés, comfortable and composed without being very sporty. Tight rear seats, uncommunicative steering and some hard plastics count against it.
Mercedes-Benz|CLE.q: Fans of comfortable coupés for long journeys, mostly for two
Mercedes-Benz|CLE.s: The CLE single-handedly replaces the former C-Class Coupé and E-Class Coupé.
Mercedes-Benz|CLE.x: The CLE 450 4MATIC appeals with its smooth, torquey six-cylinder; the CLE 300 4MATIC is livelier and better balanced in corners. The frugal, comfortable 220d is more a touring coupé than a driver's car.

Mercedes-Benz|CLE Cabriolet.v: An elegant, very well-insulated convertible that replaces the drop-top C-Class and E-Class. Tight rear seats, a modest boot and high weight temper its appeal.
p: Remarkable refinement, even with the roof down
Quick roof, operable on the move
m: Rear seats tight for tall adults
Modest boot, especially with the roof down
Mercedes-Benz|CLE Cabriolet.q: Fans of comfortable convertibles usable all year round
Mercedes-Benz|CLE Cabriolet.s: The CLE Cabriolet replaces the former C-Class and E-Class Cabriolets; its electric roof opens or closes in 20 seconds, at up to 60 km/h.

Mercedes-Benz|Classe A.v: A premium hatchback facelifted in 2023, well presented and with comprehensive MBUX infotainment, but with limited rear space and a sometimes firm ride. Its production run has been extended until 2028.
m: Over-sensitive touch controls on the steering wheel
Mercedes-Benz|Classe A.q: Single drivers or couples wanting a premium hatchback
Mercedes-Benz|Classe A.s: Once slated to be dropped, the A-Class has had its production extended until 2028; a successor on the CLA's MMA platform is expected, though not officially confirmed.
Mercedes-Benz|Classe A.x: The A200 163 hp is preferred to the A180, for identical consumption and a small price difference. The A200d 150 hp, lively and frugal on the motorway, suits high-mileage drivers.

Mercedes-Benz|Classe B.v: A practical, comfortable compact MPV, roomier than an A-Class. But the B-Class is reaching the end of its life, with no direct replacement.
m: End of production announced, uncertain resale
Imprecise touch controls on the steering wheel
Mercedes-Benz|Classe B.q: Families or seniors seeking a tall, practical premium compact
Mercedes-Benz|Classe B.s: Mercedes has announced the end of the B-Class with no direct replacement; the new GLB, available with 7 seats, fills the gap in the range.

Mercedes-Benz|Classe C.v: A comfortable, well-built premium saloon with a convincing plug-in hybrid. Facelifted in 2026, it gains newer infotainment and steering-wheel buttons, but still offers only four-cylinder engines.
p: Plug-in hybrid with around 100 km of range
m: High price even for the entry versions
Smaller boot on the plug-in hybrid
Mercedes-Benz|Classe C.q: Executives or company fleets seeking a comfortable premium saloon
Mercedes-Benz|Classe C.s: The 2026 facelift brings the new MBUX and physical buttons on the steering wheel; the diesel plug-in hybrid is dropped and an electric C-Class completes the range.
Mercedes-Benz|Classe C.x: Before the 2026 facelift, which renewed the engines, the smooth, quiet C220d 197 hp was a better bet than the noisy C200; the C300 e, which managed nearly 90 km on electric power in testing, was the most accomplished.

Mercedes-Benz|Classe C Break.v: A very comfortable, well-insulated premium estate, with a plug-in hybrid offering around 100 km of electric range. Patchy materials and high prices; the 2026 facelift brings it up to date.
p: Plug-in hybrid with around 100 km of range
m: Smaller boot on the plug-in hybrid
Mercedes-Benz|Classe C Break.q: Families or professionals wanting a frugal, comfortable premium estate
Mercedes-Benz|Classe C Break.s: The C-Class facelifted in 2026 gets the new MBUX, physical buttons on the steering wheel and a more powerful plug-in hybrid; the diesel hybrid is dropped.
Mercedes-Benz|Classe C Break.x: Before the 2026 facelift, the C220d 197 hp, smoother than the underpowered C200, offered the best compromise; the very frugal C300d e Hybrid EQ is dropped in favour of the petrol hybrids.

Mercedes-Benz|Classe C|ev.v: The first electric C-Class, the C 400 4MATIC impresses with its comfort, quietness, efficiency and very fast charging. Its high price and slightly limited cabin space temper the picture.
p: High levels of comfort and sound insulation
m: High price, quickly inflated by options
Mercedes-Benz|Classe C|ev.q: Well-off high-mileage drivers wanting a comfortable, efficient electric saloon
Mercedes-Benz|Classe C|ev.s: Compatibility with 400 V rapid chargers is a €700 option, and one worth ticking.

Mercedes-Benz|Classe E.v: A very comfortable, refined long-distance cruiser that is surprisingly agile for its weight, with advanced onboard technology. High prices and options, a smaller boot on the plug-in hybrids and unrefined four-cylinders count against it.
m: Smaller boot on the plug-in hybrids
Four-cylinders noisy when cold or revved
Mercedes-Benz|Classe E.q: High-mileage drivers or executives wanting a comfortable long-distance saloon
Mercedes-Benz|Classe E.s: The passenger screen allows video playback and videoconferencing; an electric E-Class on the MB.EA platform is announced for 2027 to replace the EQE.
Mercedes-Benz|Classe E.x: The E450d 4MATIC and its six-cylinder are the recommended version; the very frugal E220d is noisy when cold. The E300 e Hybrid EQ, comfortable and lively, loses a lot of boot space.

Mercedes-Benz|Classe E Break.v: A large premium estate with a vast boot, very comfortable and also offered in All-Terrain form, with convincing plug-in hybrids. A safe family choice, but expensive and less engaging to drive than a BMW 5 Series Touring.
m: Smaller boot on the plug-in hybrids
Mercedes-Benz|Classe E Break.q: Families or high-mileage drivers needing space and comfort
Mercedes-Benz|Classe E Break.s: The All-Terrain, raised by up to 46 mm and with 4MATIC all-wheel drive as standard, is also available as a diesel plug-in hybrid (E 300 de).
Mercedes-Benz|Classe E Break.x: The E220d is the recommended version for its versatility; the E200 four-cylinder petrol lacks refinement. The E300 e and E300d e plug-in hybrids lose boot space (460-490 l versus 615 l).

Mercedes-Benz|Classe G.v: An off-road icon with remarkable build quality, now also available as an EV. Clumsy on-road handling, modest space for its size and high running costs remain its limitations.
m: Slow steering and marked body roll on the road
Modest space and boot for its size
Electric G 580 very heavy and power-hungry
Mercedes-Benz|Classe G.q: Wealthy buyers wanting a status-symbol 4x4 that is genuinely capable off road
Mercedes-Benz|Classe G.s: The electric G 580, with four motors, can spin on the spot off road (G-Turn), but it is not approved to tow a trailer.
Mercedes-Benz|Classe G.x: The AMG G 63 is the most convincing on the road; the six-cylinder G 500 divides opinion, pleasant for one tester, sluggish off the line for another. The G 580 EQ, astonishing off road, weighs more than 3 t.

Mercedes-Benz|Classe S.v: The benchmark large luxury saloon for comfort, quietness and technology, with a long-range plug-in hybrid. The extensive 2026 facelift modernises it further, without fully restoring its aura.
m: Smaller boot on the plug-in hybrid
Unnatural regenerative braking on the hybrid
Mercedes-Benz|Classe S.q: Executives or high-mileage drivers demanding the utmost comfort
Mercedes-Benz|Classe S.s: Facelifted in early 2026 (order books opened on 30 January): half the components revised, MBUX Superscreen as standard, plug-in hybrids with around 100 km of range.
Mercedes-Benz|Classe S.x: The S580 e Hybrid EQ 4MATIC is judged the best version in the range: quiet, lively and able to cover nearly 100 km on electric power, despite inconsistent regenerative braking.

Mercedes-Benz|Classe S Limousine.v: The long-wheelbase version of the S-Class, designed for rear passengers: exceptional space, comfort and quietness, plus limousine equipment. The price, the size and the hybrid's boot hold it back.
m: Smaller boot on the plug-in hybrid
Mercedes-Benz|Classe S Limousine.q: Chauffeur-driven executives or demanding rear passengers
Mercedes-Benz|Classe S Limousine.s: Facelift revealed in late January 2026: MBUX Superscreen as standard and revised plug-in hybrids, with the S580 e rising to 585 hp.

Mercedes-Benz|EQA.v: A quiet, well-finished compact electric SUV whose range has improved since the facelift, but it is heavy, cramped in the rear and has a modest boot. The electric GLA is set to replace it.
p: Finish and equipment worthy of the brand
m: Over 2 tonnes, firm suspension on 19-inch wheels
Mercedes-Benz|EQA.q: Drivers wanting a compact premium electric SUV, mostly for two
Mercedes-Benz|EQA.s: The new electric GLA, revealed in July 2026, replaces the EQA and drops the EQ name; deliveries are announced for early 2027.

Mercedes-Benz|EQE.v: A very quiet, comfortable electric saloon with solid range and generous rear space, but divisive styling and an impractical boot. Production is due to end in 2026.
p: Very high levels of quietness and comfort
m: Saloon boot with a narrow opening
Mercedes-Benz|EQE.q: High-mileage drivers seeking a quiet electric cruiser
Mercedes-Benz|EQE.s: According to the press, production is due to end in 2026; Mercedes is preparing an electric E-Class to succeed it.

Mercedes-Benz|EQE SUV.v: A very quiet, well-equipped electric SUV with solid range, but heavy and expensive. Its ride divides opinion among testers. Production is announced to end in 2026.
Mercedes-Benz|EQE SUV.q: Well-off high-mileage drivers seeking a comfortable, quiet electric SUV
Mercedes-Benz|EQE SUV.s: According to the press, EQE production is due to end in 2026; the more recent electric GLC takes over in the range.

Mercedes-Benz|EQS.v: A very quiet, comfortable and aerodynamic electric luxury saloon with top-tier range. The 2026 facelift switches to 800 V to fix its charging, previously limited to 200 kW.
p: One of the longest ranges on the market
m: Rear access hampered by the sloping roofline
Mercedes-Benz|EQS.q: Wealthy high-mileage drivers wanting an electric limousine
Mercedes-Benz|EQS.s: The facelift presented in April 2026 adopts 800 V architecture, charging at up to 350 kW, a claimed range of up to 926 km and optional steer-by-wire.

Mercedes-Benz|EQS SUV.v: A very comfortable electric luxury SUV and a true seven-seater, with reasonable consumption for its size, but very heavy, bulky and expensive. It was designed primarily for the American market.
p: A true seven-seater, usable third row
Mercedes-Benz|EQS SUV.q: Wealthy families wanting a large, luxurious electric SUV
Mercedes-Benz|EQS SUV.s: Unlike the EQS saloon, it is built in the United States, at Mercedes' Tuscaloosa (Alabama) plant.

Mercedes-Benz|GLA.v: So far judged only as a static car, this electric GLA impresses with its careful presentation, cabin space and front boot; handling and real-world range have yet to be checked on the road.
p: Careful presentation, a clear step up in quality
Mercedes-Benz|GLA.q: Buyers of a family-oriented compact premium electric SUV
Mercedes-Benz|GLA.s: Orders opened at the end of July 2026 for the electric versions; mild-hybrid petrol versions and a 71 kWh battery are due to follow in 2027.

Mercedes-Benz|GLB.v: Electric first, the new GLB appeals with its space, seven-seat option, efficiency and very fast 800 V charging. Debatable perceived quality, touch controls and expensive options.
Mercedes-Benz|GLB.q: Families seeking a five- or seven-seat premium electric SUV
Mercedes-Benz|GLB.s: Successor to the EQB, built in Hungary. At 400 V rapid chargers, charging requires an adapter sold as an option.
Mercedes-Benz|GLB.x: The GLB 250+ 272 hp is judged the best compromise, more versatile than the GLB 200 224 hp; the GLB 350 4MATIC 354 hp adds traction and vigour, for more money.

Mercedes-Benz|GLC.v: A comfortable, quiet and well-finished premium SUV whose plug-in hybrid covers around 100 km on electric power. High weight, a boot eaten into by the battery and a bill quickly inflated by options.
p: Plug-in hybrid: around 100 km in real use
m: Heavy hybrid, thirsty with a flat battery
Smaller boot on the plug-in hybrid
Mercedes-Benz|GLC.q: Well-off families wanting a versatile, comfortable premium SUV
Mercedes-Benz|GLC.s: An all-electric GLC, without the EQ suffix, has been sold alongside it since 2026; its entry price dropped in June with the arrival of a 250 version.
Mercedes-Benz|GLC.x: The 2.0 GLC 220d 4MATIC, quiet and frugal, keeps a large boot; the GLC 300 e Hybrid EQ covers around 100 km on electric power but loses boot space and is thirsty with a flat battery.

Mercedes-Benz|GLC Coupé.v: A more stylish variant of the GLC, well insulated and effective on the road, at the cost of a smaller boot, poor rear visibility and a significant premium over the regular GLC.
Mercedes-Benz|GLC Coupé.q: Buyers who put style before space in a premium SUV

Mercedes-Benz|GLC|ev.v: A very comfortable premium electric SUV, quick to charge thanks to 800 V and with a big boot. Heavy and not very agile when driven hard, its real-world consumption falls well short of the claims and it gets expensive once optioned up.
p: 570 l boot plus 128 l front boot
m: Real-world consumption far from WLTP figures
Mercedes-Benz|GLC|ev.q: Well-off high-mileage drivers seeking a comfortable, spacious electric SUV
Mercedes-Benz|GLC|ev.s: Launched as the 400 4MATIC, the electric GLC gained two more affordable versions in June 2026, the 250 and 300 4MATIC, with an 85 kWh battery.

Mercedes-Benz|GLE.v: A comfortable, quiet and well-built large SUV, with petrol or diesel plug-in hybrids offering long electric range. Expensive, heavy and uninspiring to drive; a facelift revealed at the end of March 2026 brings it up to date.
Mercedes-Benz|GLE.q: Large families or caravanners wanting a premium SUV
Mercedes-Benz|GLE.s: A facelift revealed at the end of March 2026 (MBUX Superscreen triple display, MB.OS system) is due in the coming months: worth considering before buying.
Mercedes-Benz|GLE.x: The very heavy 2.0 GLE 350d and 400 e Hybrid EQ plug-in hybrids lose boot space and the seven-seat option; Top Gear reckons they spoil the GLE's balance.

Mercedes-Benz|GLE Coupé.v: The coupé version of the GLE: more of a status symbol, quiet and at ease on the motorway, with plug-in hybrids offering good electric range. The ride could be better in town, it is very heavy and very expensive.
p: Quiet and very comfortable on the motorway
Mercedes-Benz|GLE Coupé.q: Well-off buyers putting style first in a large premium SUV
Mercedes-Benz|GLE Coupé.s: A facelift of the GLE and GLE Coupé (MBUX Superscreen triple display, MB.OS system) was revealed at the end of March 2026: worth considering before buying.
Mercedes-Benz|GLE Coupé.x: The 3.0 GLE 450d 4MATIC, a very quiet six-cylinder, is the most refined; the 2.0 GLE 350d e Hybrid EQ runs on electric power day to day, but its diesel engine is rough.

Mercedes-Benz|GLS.v: A luxurious, well-equipped seven-seat large SUV, with a six-cylinder diesel that is powerful and frugal for its size. Bulky dimensions, high consumption in town and a very high price; a facelift was revealed in 2026.
p: High levels of luxury and equipment
m: Size makes it awkward day to day
Mercedes-Benz|GLS.q: Wealthy large families wanting a seven-seat luxury SUV
Mercedes-Benz|GLS.s: A facelift revealed at the end of March 2026 brings a larger grille, new lights and the MBUX Superscreen, still without a plug-in hybrid.

Mini|Aceman.v: An electric small SUV halfway between the Cooper and the Countryman, lively and well presented. Overly firm suspension, a small boot and a high price limit its appeal against rivals such as the Renault 5.
m: Small boot with a high loading lip
Mini|Aceman.q: City dwellers wanting a compact EV more practical than a Cooper
Mini|Aceman.s: Built in China on the same technical base as the electric Cooper; the Aceman is available only as an EV.
Mini|Aceman.x: Auto Express recommends the SE 218 hp, while L'argus finds the E 184 hp sufficient for urban use. The John Cooper Works E, expensive and still firm, fails to convince.

Mini|Cooper.v: A premium city car with strong character and an original cabin, in petrol or electric form. Tiny boot, cramped rear seats, firm suspension, patchy finish and expensive options.
p: Round OLED screen and original presentation
1.5 C responsive and frugal on the road
Mini|Cooper.q: City dwellers or couples without children wanting a fun small car
Mini|Cooper.s: The electric Coopers are built in China (in a joint venture with Great Wall); the petrol models, assembled in Oxford, keep the previous platform.
Mini|Cooper.x: The 1.5 C 156 hp, responsive and frugal, is the recommended version; the 2.0 S lacks character and the John Cooper Works disappoints. The electric SE 218 hp suffers from slow charging.

Mini|Cooper Cabrio.v: One of the last small four-seat convertibles on the market: agile, well insulated and well finished. Tiny boot, occasional rear seats and a high price; more comfortable but less playful than before.
Mini|Cooper Cabrio.q: Fans of compact convertibles for town and leisurely drives
Mini|Cooper Cabrio.s: The electric roof also works as a sunroof and operates in 18 seconds, at up to 30 km/h. The range is petrol-only.

Mini|Countryman.v: The biggest Mini, now a genuine family SUV based on the BMW X1, with combustion or electric power. Effective on the road, it is pricier than its predecessor and its build quality divides the press.
m: Build quality judged a step back by some testers
Mini|Countryman.q: Families wanting a quirky-styled compact premium SUV
Mini|Countryman.s: Built in Germany on the BMW X1's technical base, it has grown considerably in both length and height compared with the previous generation.
Mini|Countryman.x: The 1.5 C Mild Hybrid 170 hp, lively and flexible, offers the best value for money; the 2.0 S All4 adds traction, the John Cooper Works All4 extra dynamism.

Mitsubishi|ASX.v: A rebadged Renault Captur, comfortable, well finished and frugal as a hybrid, that stands out mainly for its long warranty; it costs more than its twin and runs out of breath as soon as the pace rises.
m: Hybrid noisy and overwhelmed when driven hard
Dearer than a comparable Renault Captur
Mitsubishi|ASX.q: High-mileage drivers wanting a comfortable small SUV with a long warranty
Mitsubishi|ASX.s: It shares its platform, production line and handling with the facelifted Renault Captur; the sliding rear bench lets you trade legroom for boot space.
