Mitsubishi|ASX.x: The 1.6 MPI HEV 143 hp is frugal when driven gently but struggles as soon as you accelerate; the 1.3 DI-T MHEV 140 hp with its manual gearbox seems better suited to spirited driving.

Mitsubishi|Grandis.v: A twin of the Renault Symbioz, the Grandis hybrid is a frugal, comfortable and roomy family SUV, judged competent but characterless; it stands out from its cousin mainly through its warranty.
p: Sliding rear bench and versatile boot
m: Little different from the Renault Symbioz
Mitsubishi|Grandis.q: Families wanting a frugal compact hybrid SUV with a good warranty
Mitsubishi|Grandis.s: Derived from the Renault Symbioz, whose platform and cabin it borrows, it benefits at Mitsubishi from a warranty of up to 8 years.

Mitsubishi|Outlander.v: With a bigger battery, the Outlander PHEV remains a very comfortable, well-equipped family SUV that is capable off road, and its electric range is much improved. Weight, boot and charging remain its limitations.
m: Rapid charging via CHAdeMO, which is not widespread
Mitsubishi|Outlander.q: Families wanting a comfortable large plug-in hybrid SUV with all-wheel drive
Mitsubishi|Outlander.s: Warranty of 8 years or 160,000 km. Unlike recent Renault-derived Mitsubishis, the Outlander is a pure product of the brand.

Nissan|Ariya.v: A comfortable, quiet electric SUV with a calm, well-finished cabin, fairly efficient on the open road. Its range drops sharply on the motorway, and its clumsy cornering makes it anything but engaging.
p: Good range on the open road
m: Range drops sharply on the motorway
Average boot with a high loading lip
Nissan|Ariya.q: Families wanting a comfortable, soothing electric SUV
Nissan|Ariya.s: A facelift revealed at the end of 2025 at the Tokyo Motor Show (smoothed front end, built-in Google, V2L function) arrives in Europe in 2026, with no increase in charging power.

Nissan|Juke.v: A small SUV with styling as bold as ever and a cabin modernised in 2024, plus a hybrid that is frugal in town. The sometimes hesitant hybrid gearbox, the rear space and the hybrid's boot remain below par.
Nissan|Juke.q: Style-conscious city dwellers who mostly drive in town
Nissan|Juke.s: A new-generation all-electric Juke, built in Sunderland, is expected at the end of 2026; the petrol Juke is set to sit alongside it for many months.
Nissan|Juke.x: The 1.6 Hybrid 143 hp, smoother and more frugal in town, avoids the French malus tax but costs significantly more than the 114 hp 1.0 petrol and sacrifices boot space.

Nissan|Leaf.v: An EV pioneer, the Leaf becomes a comfortable, quiet and well-connected crossover. Its real-world consumption is well above the claimed figure, and its price, fair for some, remains a little high for others.
m: Real-world consumption above the claimed figure
Tight rear seats for tall occupants
Slower charging with the small battery
Nissan|Leaf.q: Families wanting a comfortable, well-connected compact EV
Nissan|Leaf.s: This third generation drops the hatchback for a crossover on the Ariya's platform; it is built in the UK and supports bidirectional charging.
Nissan|Leaf.x: The Extended Range 217 hp accelerates better and charges faster (150 kW); the Standard Range 177 hp is limited to 105 kW for rapid charging.

Nissan|Micra.v: An electric city car twinned with the Renault 5, with neat styling, lively handling and a well-executed Google infotainment system. Rear space is tight and it costs at least as much as its cousin.
m: Limited rapid charging on the smaller battery
Nissan|Micra.q: Urban drivers wanting a compact EV with original styling
Nissan|Micra.s: A technical twin of the Renault 5 E-Tech, from which it borrows most of its cabin, the Micra stands apart mainly through its exterior styling.
Nissan|Micra.x: The Long Range 150 hp, livelier and quicker to charge, is judged the best choice; the Standard Range 120 hp is limited to 80 kW on rapid charging.

Nissan|Qashqai.v: The pioneer and best-seller of the compact SUV class, well built and offering an e-Power system that drives very much like an EV, revised in 2025 to be more frugal and quieter. Comfort suffers on 20-inch wheels.
p: Smooth e-Power with a very EV-like drive
m: Rear seats and boot merely average
Nissan|Qashqai.q: Families looking for a versatile compact SUV with no plugging in
Nissan|Qashqai.s: Built in Sunderland, the Qashqai gained a second-generation e-Power in 2025, claimed to be 16% more frugal and quieter under acceleration.

Nissan|X-Trail.v: A large family SUV with a smooth, quiet e-Power powertrain and an e-4ORCE drivetrain that adds to its appeal. Disappointing motorway economy, an occasional-use third row and a heavy French malus tax.
p: Up to 7 seats, wide rear doors
m: No economy advantage on the motorway
Nissan|X-Trail.q: Large families wanting a spacious hybrid SUV with no plugging in
Nissan|X-Trail.s: Facelifted in 2026 (Google built in). A fifth generation, unveiled in April 2026, is due first in the United States in 2027; Europe may have to wait until 2028.

Opel|Astra.v: A sister to the Peugeot 308 with more conventional ergonomics, the facelifted Astra remains comfortable and frugal in everyday use. The changes are modest and the press finds the electric version expensive.
p: Physical controls, easy to get to grips with
m: Tight rear seats for anyone over 1.75 m
145 hp hybrid thirsty on the motorway
Electric version expensive and slow to charge
Opel|Astra.q: Drivers wanting a sensible hatchback with conventional ergonomics
Opel|Astra.s: Facelifted in 2026: electric range raised to 454 km WLTP with a V2L function, a 195 hp plug-in hybrid and Intelli-Seats with a central recess.
Opel|Astra.x: The 145 hp hybrid, the cheapest, is smooth and frugal in town but thirsty on the motorway; the diesel remains the most economical for high-mileage drivers; the electric version, economical, is judged too expensive.

Opel|Astra Sports Tourer.v: The Astra estate keeps the hatchback's strengths, comfort and simple ergonomics, and adds a practical boot with a low sill. More practical than dynamic, it is less lively than a Peugeot 308 SW.
m: 145 hp hybrid thirsty on the motorway
Opel|Astra Sports Tourer.q: Families or high-mileage drivers needing space without switching to an SUV
Opel|Astra Sports Tourer.s: Facelifted in early 2026 along with the Astra: revised front end, Intelli-Seats and increased range for the electric version.
Opel|Astra Sports Tourer.x: The 145 hp hybrid is smooth and frugal in town but thirsty on the motorway; the diesel remains the choice for high-mileage drivers; the electric version, economical, is judged expensive.

Opel|Corsa.v: A cousin of the Peugeot 208 with a more conventional cabin, the Corsa relies on simple ergonomics and a wide choice of powertrains. Agile but firm, it is showing its age inside.
p: Physical controls, easy to get to grips with
Choice of petrol, hybrid or electric
Opel|Corsa.q: Urban drivers wanting a simple all-rounder, whatever the powertrain
Opel|Corsa.s: 48V hybrids built between June 2023 and January 2026 were recalled in 2026 (fire risk). A new all-electric Corsa is expected around 2028.
Opel|Corsa.x: The 48V hybrid struggles to justify its extra cost against full hybrids; the electric GSE, lively and effective on track, struggles to reach 300 km of real-world range.

Opel|Frontera.v: A twin of the Citroën C3 Aircross, the Frontera offers lots of space for a modest price. The hybrid is smooth, but the sound insulation and build quality betray the cost-cutting.
p: Smooth hybrid with decent mid-range pull
Opel|Frontera.q: Families on a tight budget who put space before finish
Opel|Frontera.s: Recalls in 2026: power steering (built February-May 2025) and 48V hybrids built up to January 2026 (fire risk).

Opel|Grandland.v: A cousin of the Peugeot 3008, with which it shares its platform, the Grandland focuses on space, comfort and understated styling. Rational rather than exciting, it is best recommended as the 145 hp hybrid.
Opel|Grandland.q: Families wanting a spacious SUV without the 3008's bold design choices
Opel|Grandland.s: Opel warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km since June 2025, extended with each service carried out within the Opel network.
Opel|Grandland.x: The 145 hp hybrid (which replaces the 136 hp tested by the press), the most affordable, is enough for family use but uses more fuel than claimed; the Electric 73 kWh 213 hp, much more expensive, mainly makes sense for high-mileage drivers.

Opel|Mokka.v: The Mokka wins people over first with its styling, bolder than that of its Peugeot 2008 and Jeep Avenger cousins. Agile and enjoyable in town, its boot remains tight for a family.
p: Easy to manoeuvre in town, agile on the road
Electric version focused on comfort and ergonomics
m: Slow-reacting automatic gearbox on the hybrid
Opel|Mokka.q: Urban drivers or small households who care about design
Opel|Mokka.s: 48V hybrids built between June 2023 and January 2026 were recalled in 2026 (fire risk). Opel warranty of up to 8 years with servicing in the network.

Opel|Mokka GSE.v: The sporty electric version of the Mokka, with a stiffened chassis, Alcon brakes and a limited-slip differential. Quick and precise, especially on track, but firm, short on feedback on the road and held back by its real-world range.
m: Limited real-world range when driven hard
Opel|Mokka GSE.q: Keen drivers who mostly drive in town and the suburbs
Opel|Mokka GSE.s: Shares its platform and electric powertrain with the Abarth 600e and the Alfa Romeo Junior Veloce.

Peugeot|2008.v: The 2008 remains a benchmark among small SUVs thanks to its cabin presentation and generous boot. In 2026 it gains the chain-driven Turbo 100, but the i-Cockpit still divides opinion.
m: Divisive i-Cockpit with small steering wheel
Peugeot|2008.q: Small families looking for a well-presented compact SUV
Peugeot|2008.s: 48V hybrids built between June 2023 and January 2026 were recalled in 2026 (fire risk). Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years.

Peugeot|208.v: European Car of the Year 2020, the 208 remains one of the best-presented city cars. The small-wheeled i-Cockpit does not suit everyone and rear space is tight.
m: i-Cockpit not suited to every body size
Peugeot|208.q: Urban drivers who care about styling and interior presentation
Peugeot|208.s: A new all-electric 208 is expected in the second half of 2027; the current car should stay in the range in petrol and hybrid form.

Peugeot|3008.v: The third-generation 3008 adopts a fastback silhouette and a large curved panoramic screen. A well-finished cabin and reasonable economy, but the 145 hp hybrid lacks punch and rear space disappoints.
p: Quiet on the motorway, reasonable economy
m: Modest performance from the 145 hp hybrid
Peugeot|3008.q: Families wanting an SUV with bold design and a well-finished interior
Peugeot|3008.s: Only four stars from Euro NCAP. Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km, provided the car is serviced within the Peugeot network.
Peugeot|3008.x: The 145 hp hybrid is adequate for everyday use without sparkle and its three-cylinder is audible; the 225 hp plug-in hybrid, much livelier and able to run on electric power, costs more.

Peugeot|308.v: Facelifted in 2025, the 308 remains one of the best-presented hatchbacks, with an effective chassis and good sound insulation. Rising prices, a noisy three-cylinder and the much-debated i-Cockpit temper its appeal.
p: Good sound insulation on the motorway
m: Visibility of the i-Cockpit instrument cluster
Peugeot|308.q: Drivers who demand a well-presented cabin and an enjoyable drive
Peugeot|308.s: Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km, provided the car is serviced within the Peugeot network.

Peugeot|308 SW.v: The 308 SW estate adds a very practical boot to the hatchback. An elegant, dynamic family car, with a cabin barely changed in the facelift, a still-debated i-Cockpit and a 145 hp hybrid that is a little short of breath when loaded.
Peugeot|308 SW.q: Families who prefer a well-presented estate to an SUV
Peugeot|308 SW.s: Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km, provided the car is serviced within the Peugeot network.
Peugeot|308 SW.x: The 145 hp hybrid, the most affordable, struggles a little when the estate is loaded; the 195 hp plug-in hybrid loses more than 100 litres of boot space to its battery.

Peugeot|408.v: Somewhere between saloon and SUV, the facelifted 408 stands out for its lines, its comfort and a welcoming rear cabin. An original choice, but expensive, with questionable ergonomics and a sluggish 145 hp hybrid.
m: Instrument cluster partly hidden by the steering wheel
Peugeot|408.q: Drivers wanting an original family car without opting for an SUV
Peugeot|408.s: Facelifted in 2026: revised front end and the plug-in hybrid raised to 240 hp. The three-claw headlights and illuminated badge are reserved for GT trims.
Peugeot|408.x: The 145 hp hybrid is adequate without being quick and is noisier; the 240 hp plug-in hybrid is much livelier, but its engine makes itself heard under acceleration.

Peugeot|5008.v: The 5008 swaps its MPV look for that of an SUV and keeps seven seats as standard. A well-finished cabin and relaxing drive, but the third row is tight for adults and the 145 hp hybrid lacks sparkle.
Peugeot|5008.q: Large families looking for a versatile seven-seat SUV
Peugeot|5008.s: Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km, provided the car is serviced within the Peugeot network.
Peugeot|5008.x: The 145 hp hybrid is adequate without sparkle but remains the smoothest version; the 225 hp plug-in hybrid brings considerably more vigour.

Peugeot|e-2008.v: The e-2008 offers well-judged comfort, a smooth drive and decent range on open roads. But it is expensive against its rivals and its combustion-engined sibling, and its range melts away on the motorway.
p: Practical boot with a flat floor
Peugeot|e-2008.q: Small families switching to electric and charging at home
Peugeot|e-2008.s: Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km, provided the car is serviced within the Peugeot network.

Peugeot|e-208.v: The e-208 combines a flattering cabin with agile handling. But the boot and rear seats are tight, rapid charging lags behind and recent rivals offer better value for money.
Peugeot|e-208.q: Urban or suburban drivers who can charge at home
Peugeot|e-208.s: Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km, provided the car is serviced within the Peugeot network.
Peugeot|e-208.x: The 156 hp, barely quicker than the 136 hp, stands out for its better range; the GTi 280 hp gains a limited-slip differential and a revised chassis.

Peugeot|e-3008.v: The e-3008 stands out for a range among the best on the market in Long Range form and a well-finished, quiet cabin. Firm suspension, tight rear seats and lacklustre performance in 210 hp form.
p: Class-leading range with the large battery
Peugeot|e-3008.q: High-mileage drivers ready to go electric without compromising on range
Peugeot|e-3008.s: Only four stars from Euro NCAP. Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km, provided the car is serviced within the Peugeot network.
Peugeot|e-3008.x: The 210 hp is adequate and remains the most coherent choice; the 230 hp Long Range accelerates barely any better but goes much further; the 4x4 325 hp, the liveliest, has the shortest range.

Peugeot|e-308.v: The e-308 combines the 308's presentation and comfort with restrained electricity consumption. A well-rounded hatchback, but expensive and behind the competition on both range and charging.
p: Carefully judged comfort and build quality
m: Instrument cluster partly hidden by the steering wheel
Peugeot|e-308.q: EV drivers who prefer a low-slung hatchback to an SUV
Peugeot|e-308.s: Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km, provided the car is serviced within the Peugeot network.

Peugeot|e-308 SW.v: The e-308 SW combines a large boot, agile handling and good sound insulation. A rare electric family car that is not an SUV, let down by modest motorway range and unremarkable rapid charging.
p: A rare electric estate on the market
Peugeot|e-308 SW.q: Families going electric who prefer an estate to an SUV
Peugeot|e-308 SW.s: Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km, provided the car is serviced within the Peugeot network.

Peugeot|e-408.v: The e-408 brings the 408's distinctive lines to an electric powertrain, with very restrained consumption and a comfortable chassis. Lagging rapid charging and dated technology for the price limit its appeal.
Peugeot|e-408.q: EV drivers wanting to stand out from the SUV crowd
Peugeot|e-408.s: Facelifted in 2026 with a revised front end; battery and range remain close to the pre-facelift figures.

Peugeot|e-5008.v: The e-5008 offers seven seats and a comfortable range, a rare combination in an EV. It weighs more than two tonnes and is less flexible than the previous generation.
m: Weight of more than two tonnes
Peugeot|e-5008.q: Large families ready to switch to electric
Peugeot|e-5008.s: Peugeot Care warranty of up to 8 years or 160,000 km since June 2025, with servicing every two years within the Peugeot network.

Porsche|911 (992).v: The facelifted 911 remains the benchmark all-round sports car: precise steering, a disciplined chassis, lively engines. Hybridisation adds vigour to the GTS without betraying its character; the bill remains hefty.
p: Precise steering and a highly disciplined chassis
Near-instant engine response from the GTS T-Hybrid
m: Firm suspension and pronounced road noise
No more manual gearbox on the GTS hybrid
Porsche|911 (992).q: Demanding sports car enthusiasts who also want to use it every day
Porsche|911 (992).s: The GTS T-Hybrid is not a plug-in: its small battery charges on the move and the car never runs on electric power alone. The hybrid system is there for performance.
Porsche|911 (992).x: The Carrera appeals with its balance; the manual Carrera T is rawer. The GTS T-Hybrid, heavier and firmer, is much livelier. The naturally aspirated GT3 targets the track but remains liveable.

Porsche|Cayenne.v: The dynamic benchmark among large luxury SUVs, the facelifted Cayenne impresses with its chassis, build quality and wide range; the new Cayenne Electric inherits these qualities, but options quickly push up the bill.
p: Handling among the best in the class
Smooth, muscular V8 in the S and GTS
m: Electric: AC charging limited to 11 kW
Electric: real-world consumption well above the claim
Porsche|Cayenne.q: Well-off families wanting a large, versatile SUV that is effective on the road
Porsche|Cayenne.s: The Cayenne Electric, launched in 2026 on a new platform, is sold alongside the petrol and plug-in hybrid versions facelifted in 2023.
Porsche|Cayenne.x: The 4.0 S 474 hp is judged smooth and lively, the GTS more vocal; the 3.0 353 hp is refined but less spirited. More recent, the Electric 408 hp impresses with its chassis and rapid charging, less so with its range.

Porsche|Cayenne Coupé.v: Mechanically identical to the Cayenne, the Coupé combines top-level comfort and roadholding, from the E-Hybrid to the Turbo Electric, but costs more and sacrifices boot space for a dynamic gain judged slight.
p: Remarkable balance of comfort and roadholding
Rear seats still welcoming for adults
Careful build quality and modern cabin
m: Boot much smaller than the Cayenne's
Dearer than the Cayenne for similar qualities
Plug-in hybrid dull once the battery is flat
Porsche|Cayenne Coupé.q: Style-conscious buyers wanting a more exclusive Cayenne, with no need for a big boot
Porsche|Cayenne Coupé.s: Two rear seats as standard, a third as an option. Since 2026, an electric version has joined the petrol and plug-in hybrid Coupés facelifted in 2023.
Porsche|Cayenne Coupé.x: The 3.0 E-Hybrid 470 hp is comfortable but lacks punch with the battery flat; the 4.0 GTS 500 hp is firmer and more communicative; the Turbo Electric 857 hp impresses with its comfort and performance.

Porsche|Macan.v: Now electric, the Macan keeps the agility and precision expected of a Porsche despite its weight, with convincing rapid charging and range; expensive options and no one-pedal driving.
p: Agile chassis and precise steering despite the weight
m: No one-pedal driving, little regenerative braking
Limited rear headroom for tall passengers
Porsche|Macan.q: Driving enthusiasts going electric without giving up the fun
Porsche|Macan.s: The electric Macan shares its PPE platform with the Audi Q6 e-tron; a front boot of around 84 litres adds to the main boot.
Porsche|Macan.x: The Electric 360 hp (rear-wheel drive) is judged the most recommendable, agile and long-legged; the 4 Electric 408 hp is mainly useful in the mountains; the 4S Electric 516 hp is more playful, the Turbo Electric better finished.

Porsche|Panamera.v: The Panamera remains the benchmark large sporting saloon, blending luxury and dynamism; the plug-in hybrids, the only versions to get Active Ride suspension, are the most accomplished.
p: Top-tier build quality and interior presentation
m: Limited boot, especially on the hybrids
Tight rear knee room, firm seatbacks
Porsche|Panamera.q: Well-off high-mileage drivers looking for a sporty luxury saloon
Porsche|Panamera.s: 25.9 kWh battery on the hybrids, with no DC rapid charging. At launch, the French malus tax made the petrol Panamera more expensive than the plug-in hybrid.
Porsche|Panamera.x: The 2.9 353 hp is agile but quiet and fairly firm; the 2.9 4 E-Hybrid 470 hp is refined but a little dull, the 4S E-Hybrid livelier; the GTS has the most expressive engine, the Turbo E-Hybrid is impressive.

Porsche|Taycan.v: The facelifted Taycan gains significantly in range and charging speed without losing any of its driving appeal. The press judges it highly accomplished but points to very high prices and options.
p: Very fast charging, up to 320 kW
Much-improved range, frugal on the motorway
m: Weight felt at the limit, inconsistent braking
Porsche|Taycan.q: Enthusiasts wanting a sporty electric grand tourer, with a very generous budget
Porsche|Taycan.s: In testing, the rear-wheel-drive version covered Lyon to Paris (500 km) with a single 5-minute stop. The British press warns of heavy depreciation.
Porsche|Taycan.x: The rear-wheel-drive Electric Performance Plus 435 hp, frugal and quick enough, offers the best value for money; the 4 is reassuring in snow. The Turbo and Turbo S, very heavy, sacrifice involvement.

Porsche|Taycan Cross Turismo.v: The most versatile Taycan: as capable as the saloon, more comfortable and roomier in the back. The press judges it highly accomplished, but expensive, not very spacious for an estate and not built for off-roading.
p: More rear headroom than the saloon
m: Real-world motorway range far from the claim
Porsche|Taycan Cross Turismo.q: Well-off families wanting a fast electric estate that can handle tracks
Porsche|Taycan Cross Turismo.s: Ground clearance raised by 20 mm and a Gravel mode, without making it a true off-roader. Neither GTS nor Turbo GT in this body style.
Porsche|Taycan Cross Turismo.x: The 4S Electric Performance Plus 598 hp, quick enough, is the best compromise according to CAR and Top Gear; the Turbo and Turbo S are over the top, the Turbo S being the least frugal.

Porsche|Taycan Sport Turismo.v: The same qualities as the facelifted saloon, with a slightly more practical shooting brake silhouette. The press often prefers it to the saloon and praises its handling, but its boot remains small.
p: Charging up to 320 kW, increased range
More practical than the saloon for a small premium
m: Modest boot and narrow rear seats
Porsche|Taycan Sport Turismo.q: Demanding drivers wanting a sporty electric estate for moderate family use
Porsche|Taycan Sport Turismo.s: Unlike the Cross Turismo, it has neither raised ground clearance nor body protection. The press mainly tested the GTS version.
Porsche|Taycan Sport Turismo.x: The GTS Electric 700 hp, the sharpest, makes the Turbo S superfluous for everyday use according to evo, but is expensive: evo and Motoring Research consider the entry-level rear-wheel-drive version the wiser choice.

Renault|4 E-Tech.v: A neo-retro electric small SUV, more practical than the Renault 5 thanks to its boot, and comfortable. But the rear is narrow for three, range drops sharply on the motorway and the price is high.
p: Bigger boot than the R5, low sill
m: Floor not flat with the rear bench folded
Renault|4 E-Tech.q: Young urban families looking for a practical EV
Renault|4 E-Tech.s: It uses the technical base of the Renault 5 E-Tech. Only the 150 hp gets regenerative braking paddles and the folding front passenger seat.
Renault|4 E-Tech.x: The Urban Range 120 hp is only one second slower from 0-100 km/h and is sufficient according to Le Moniteur Automobile, but its small battery limits range; the Comfort Range 150 hp opens up the better-equipped trims.

Renault|5 E-Tech.v: An electric city car with successful neo-retro styling, voted European Car of the Year 2025. Pleasant to drive and well equipped, it falls short on rear space, storage and a high price for the class.
Renault|5 E-Tech.q: Urban drivers looking for a stylish EV that is enjoyable to drive
Renault|5 E-Tech.s: Voted European Car of the Year 2025 jointly with the Alpine A290, alongside which it is built in Douai (northern France).

Renault|Austral.v: Facelifted in 2025 and refocused on the 200 hp E-Tech hybrid, the Austral gains in comfort and presentation and remains agile, especially with rear-wheel steering. One of the better choices among hybrid SUVs.
Renault|Austral.q: Families looking for a frugal, comfortable hybrid SUV
Renault|Austral.s: 2025 facelift: revised front end, driver monitoring camera and the end of the 130 and 160 hp mild hybrid versions. Built in Palencia (Spain).

Renault|Captur.v: Facelifted in 2024, the Captur remains a versatile small SUV, with a sliding rear bench, a well-executed Google interface and a rare LPG option. The hybrid loses boot space and makes itself heard when driven hard.
p: Decent equipment from the entry-level version
Renault|Captur.q: Urban families looking for a versatile, frugal small SUV
Renault|Captur.s: The Eco-G version runs on LPG and petrol: LPG remains cheaper than petrol at the pump.
Renault|Captur.x: The 1.2 Eco-G 120 hp, barely dearer than the petrol, is judged to pay for itself quickly thanks to the price of LPG; the hybrid, frugal and quiet in town, loses boot space and is audible on hills.

Renault|Clio.v: The Clio 6 improves in style, equipment and economy with its 160 hp hybrid. But rear space and the boot have barely changed, and the hybrid lacks punch and refinement at high speed.
m: No notable improvement in rear space
Renault|Clio.q: Urban and suburban drivers looking for a frugal city car
Renault|Clio.s: It retains the Clio 5's CMF-B platform and is built in Turkey. A 120 hp LPG version completes the range.

Renault|Espace.v: Now an SUV and facelifted in 2025, the Espace is comfortable, well finished and frugal as a hybrid. But its cramped third row and limited flexibility set it apart from the MPV of old.
Renault|Espace.q: Families wanting a large, comfortable hybrid SUV
Renault|Espace.s: 2025 facelift: revised front end and better engine insulation. The seven-seat version costs around €1,000 more.

Renault|Megane E-Tech.v: Facelifted in 2026, the electric Mégane simplifies its range and gains an LFP battery, a little more range and faster charging, at a lower price. Progress judged modest against the competition.
m: No large battery, unlike the Scénic
Renault|Megane E-Tech.q: Drivers wanting a well-equipped electric hatchback
Renault|Megane E-Tech.s: 2026 facelift: a single 67 kWh LFP battery, a 220 hp motor and a claimed 15-80% charge in 24 minutes.

Renault|Rafale.v: Renault's upmarket coupé-SUV, convincing in its handling. The 300 hp plug-in hybrid, smooth and frugal, offers genuine electric range, but its three-cylinder engine and price are debatable.
p: Electric range useful day to day
Renault|Rafale.q: Executives looking for a prestige hybrid SUV at a lower cost
Renault|Rafale.s: The 300 hp version adds a rear electric motor, and its Atelier Alpine trim adds camera-controlled suspension. No DC rapid charging.
Renault|Rafale.x: The 1.2 Hyper Hybrid E-Tech 4x4 300 hp is livelier, more comfortable and covers around 100 km on electric power; it costs around €5,500 more than the 200 hp and uses a little more fuel with the battery flat.

Renault|Scenic E-Tech.v: European Car of the Year 2024, the electric Scénic appeals with its cabin space, range and comfort. Its rapid charging is merely average and it is less flexible than earlier Scénics.
m: High price of the large battery
Renault|Scenic E-Tech.q: Families wanting an EV for long journeys
Renault|Scenic E-Tech.s: Voted European Car of the Year 2024. It is built in Douai (northern France).

Renault|Symbioz.v: Slotting in between the Captur and Austral, the Symbioz offers a bigger boot than the Captur and a frugal, better-geared 160 hp hybrid. But it shares the Captur's wheelbase, and therefore its rear space.
m: Rear space identical to the Captur
Little-changed cabin, close to the Captur's
Gearbox less responsive than a dual-clutch
Renault|Symbioz.q: Families wanting a Captur with a more practical boot
Renault|Symbioz.s: It shares the CMF-B platform and wheelbase of the Captur, with a longer rear overhang. It is built in Spain.
Renault|Symbioz.x: The 1.8 Full Hybrid E-Tech 160 hp, more frugal and free of the French malus tax, is judged preferable to the 1.3 Mild Hybrid 140 hp, cheaper to buy but thirstier and manual-only.

Renault|Twingo.v: The Twingo returns as an EV, very keenly priced, frugal and flexible thanks to its sliding rear bench. Rapid charging as a paid option and range tailored to the city limit how far it can go.
m: Basic sound insulation and build quality
Renault|Twingo.q: Urban drivers wanting a brand-new EV at the lowest possible price
Renault|Twingo.s: Assembled in Novo Mesto (Slovenia) on the Renault 5's technical base, with a 27.5 kWh LFP battery. Rapid charging comes as part of an optional pack.

Seat|Arona.v: A small SUV derived from the Ibiza, facelifted for 2026: pleasant to drive, roomy, better finished and well equipped. Still no hybrid option, a handicap against the Captur and 2008.
Seat|Arona.q: Urban families looking for a small petrol SUV
Seat|Arona.s: Facelift on sale since January 2026, with the range reduced to Copa and FR trims. A mild hybrid system is due in 2027.
Seat|Arona.x: The 1.0 TSI 116 hp is judged the best compromise; the 1.5 TSI Evo2 150 hp, rougher, hardly feels any quicker in everyday driving.

Seat|Ateca.v: A compact SUV liked for its handling and boot, but whose design dates back to 2016. Production ended in 2026, with no direct replacement.
Seat|Ateca.q: Buyers hunting for a good deal on a stock car
Seat|Ateca.s: Production ended at the end of April 2026 in Kvasiny (Czech Republic); Seat has no direct replacement planned. Sold from stock only.

Seat|Ibiza.v: A city car facelifted for 2026, with a revised front end and improved materials, still pleasant to drive, better equipped but more expensive. The lack of a hybrid option counts against it versus rivals such as the Clio.
p: One of the better boots in the segment
Seat|Ibiza.q: Drivers looking for a simple, well-equipped petrol city car
Seat|Ibiza.s: Facelift on sale since January 2026, with the range reduced to Copa and FR trims. A mild hybrid system is due in 2027.
Seat|Ibiza.x: The 1.0 TSI 95 hp is enough for most uses, the 1.0 TSI 116 hp is more at ease on the motorway; the 1.5 TSI Evo2 150 hp is judged too expensive.

Seat|Leon.v: A hatchback cousin of the Golf, more stylish and cheaper for similar qualities, with a very wide engine range. The 2024 facelift brought a larger screen, but touch controls remain plentiful.
p: Plug-in hybrid with excellent electric range
m: Smaller boot on the plug-in hybrid
Seat|Leon.q: Drivers wanting a sportier, cheaper Golf
Seat|Leon.s: It shares its platform and engines with the VW Golf. A full hybrid version is due in 2028.
Seat|Leon.x: The 2.0 TDI 150 hp, quiet and very frugal, suits high-mileage drivers; the 1.5 eHybrid 204 hp covers more than 100 km on electric power but loses boot space; the petrol and mild hybrid versions are lively in town.

Seat|Leon Sportstourer.v: A compact estate with a very generous boot, more agile and more frugal than an SUV. A serious rival to the Octavia Combi and Golf Estate, with a full choice of engines, but too reliant on touch controls.
p: One of the biggest boots around
Plug-in hybrid with excellent electric range
Seat|Leon Sportstourer.q: Families wanting a versatile estate, diesel or plug-in hybrid
Seat|Leon Sportstourer.s: It shares its platform and engines with the VW Golf and Skoda Octavia. A full hybrid version is due in 2028.
Seat|Leon Sportstourer.x: The 2.0 TDI 150 hp is frugal on long journeys; the 1.5 eHybrid 204 hp covers more than 100 km on electric power but sacrifices some boot space.

Skoda|Elroq.v: A compact electric SUV that brings the Enyaq's practical qualities to a shorter format at a reasonable price. Rational and efficient, it feels firm without adaptive dampers.
m: Modest range on the entry-level version
No regenerative braking paddles on the entry-level version
Skoda|Elroq.q: Families wanting a compact, roomy electric SUV
Skoda|Elroq.s: Runner-up in the 2026 European Car of the Year, behind the Mercedes CLA.
Skoda|Elroq.x: The 55 kWh 170 hp is mainly suited to town use; the 63 kWh 204 hp is the best compromise according to Caroom; the 82 kWh 286 hp is livelier and goes further. The 4x4 is aimed at snowy regions.

Skoda|Elroq RS.v: The all-wheel-drive version of the Elroq, quicker without losing the base model's space. Not much fun for a performance model, it costs considerably more than the standard versions.
m: High price compared with the standard versions
Not much fun to drive, prone to understeer
Skoda|Elroq RS.q: Families wanting a compact, high-performance electric SUV

Skoda|Enyaq.v: A comfortable, very well insulated electric family SUV, facelifted in 2025. It focuses on space and comfort, at the cost of weak brakes and high winter consumption on the motorway.
m: Price still high despite the cut
High winter consumption on the motorway
Skoda|Enyaq.q: Families making long journeys by EV
Skoda|Enyaq.s: Facelifted in 2025 (“Modern Solid” front end, drag coefficient cut to 0.245), it has seen its price fall by more than €7,000 in France.

Skoda|Enyaq Coupé.v: A sloping-roof version of the Enyaq, more aerodynamic and with slightly more range, without sacrificing interior space. But its extra cost makes it less rational than the regular SUV.
m: Extra cost over the regular Enyaq
Skoda|Enyaq Coupé.q: Style-conscious buyers wanting an electric family SUV
Skoda|Enyaq Coupé.s: Facelifted in 2025 along with the Enyaq, it has a drag coefficient of 0.225, against 0.245 for the SUV version.

Skoda|Enyaq Coupé RS.v: The fastest Enyaq accelerates hard and remains comfortable, quiet and well finished, but the press finds it too tame to drive for an RS, and its extra cost over an Enyaq 85x hard to justify.
p: Careful build quality, boot barely reduced by the sloping roof
m: Brakes hard to modulate, pedal lacks bite
High price against less powerful Enyaqs
Skoda|Enyaq Coupé RS.q: Buyers wanting a fast, comfortable electric coupé-SUV rather than a sporty one
Skoda|Enyaq Coupé RS.s: Verdict based on tests of the Coupé RS and, in Car Magazine's case, the Enyaq RS (SUV) with the same powertrain. Top speed limited to 180 km/h.

Skoda|Enyaq RS.v: The all-wheel-drive version of the Enyaq, fast without giving up the family SUV's comfort and space. But it is barely any sportier than the standard versions, for a considerably higher price.
p: One of the biggest boots in its class
Skoda|Enyaq RS.q: Families looking for a fast, spacious electric SUV
Skoda|Enyaq RS.s: Facelifted in 2025, mainly cosmetically. According to Auto Express, it is only just over a second quicker than the Enyaq 85x.

Skoda|Epiq.v: A practical, comfortable small electric SUV, praised for its boot, rear space and price. Its rapid charging is merely average and its interior presentation simple.
Skoda|Epiq.q: Families looking for a practical, affordable small electric SUV
Skoda|Epiq.s: Shares its technical base (front-wheel-drive MEB+) with the VW ID. Polo and Cupra Raval. Two-year Skoda manufacturer warranty.

Skoda|Fabia.v: One of the most spacious and practical city cars in its class, comfortable and easy to live with. Unlike the Clio or 208, it offers no electrified powertrain.
p: Comfortable suspension, though soft on poor roads
m: Entry-level MPI 80 hp best kept to town use
Skoda|Fabia.q: Small families wanting a roomy, sensible city car

Skoda|Kamiq.v: A sensible small SUV, spacious and comfortable, that puts practicality before style. Against increasingly electrified competition, it suffers from the lack of any hybrid option.
p: Generous interior space, especially in the rear
m: Average boot, no sliding rear bench
Skoda|Kamiq.q: Families looking for a practical, no-surprises small SUV
Skoda|Kamiq.s: Facelifted in 2024, it shares its technical base with the VW T-Cross and Seat Arona.

Skoda|Karoq.v: A practical, proven compact SUV, comfortable and well insulated, with rare interior flexibility. Its 2022 facelift was cautious and it still offers no hybrid version.
p: Comfort and sound insulation on long journeys
m: Entry-level 1.0 TSI short of breath when loaded
Skoda|Karoq.q: Drivers wanting a practical, flexible compact SUV
Skoda|Karoq.s: Facelifted in early 2022: wider grille, Matrix LED lights and more driver aids, while the interior changed little.

Skoda|Kodiaq.v: A spacious, comfortable and well-insulated large family SUV, with optional seven seats and a huge boot. A rational benchmark against the Peugeot 5008, even if the 150 hp diesel runs short of breath when loaded.
p: Very generous cabin space and boot
m: 150 hp diesel a little short of breath when loaded
Plug-in hybrid limited to five seats
Skoda|Kodiaq.q: Large families looking for a spacious, comfortable SUV
Skoda|Kodiaq.s: It shares its technical base (MQB Evo) with the VW Tayron. The plug-in hybrid has a claimed electric range of more than 100 km. Two-year warranty.
Skoda|Kodiaq.x: The 1.5 TSI Hybrid 150 hp is the choice recommended by Carbuyer; the 204 hp PHEV, livelier than expected and long-legged on electric power, only has five seats; the 2.0 TDI 150 hp runs short of breath when loaded.

Skoda|Kodiaq RS.v: The sporty petrol version of the Kodiaq, which keeps the space and seven seats while adding solid performance. But it is not much fun, uses considerably more fuel than the diesel and is expensive.
m: Considerably dearer than the regular Kodiaq
Barely more fun than a regular Kodiaq
Skoda|Kodiaq RS.q: Families wanting a high-performance large SUV
Skoda|Kodiaq RS.s: It uses the VW Golf GTI's 2.0 TSI and can tow 2.5 tonnes. Two-year Skoda manufacturer warranty.

Skoda|Octavia.v: One of the roomiest compact saloons on the market, with an estate-sized boot and careful build quality. Facelifted in 2024, it remains a rational benchmark, with no plug-in hybrid for now.
p: Restrained consumption in mild hybrid form
m: Too many functions via the touchscreen
Skoda|Octavia.q: High-mileage drivers or families looking for space and economy
Skoda|Octavia.s: Facelifted in 2024, it shares its technical base with the VW Golf. Two-year Skoda manufacturer warranty.
Skoda|Octavia.x: The 1.5 TSI Hybrid DSG7 versions, assisted by mild hybrid tech, make up for the manual versions' lack of low-rev pulling power; the 2.0 TDI remains the most frugal.

Skoda|Octavia Combi.v: The benchmark compact estate for space, with a 640-litre boot and generous rear room. Frugal in mild hybrid form, comfortable on the motorway and well finished, it does however become expensive in higher trims.
p: One of the biggest boots in the segment
Restrained consumption in mild hybrid form
Skoda|Octavia Combi.q: Families or business users needing space
Skoda|Octavia Combi.s: Facelifted in 2024, it is due for a second facelift. Two-year Skoda manufacturer warranty, shorter than those of Asian brands.

Skoda|Octavia Combi RS.v: A sporty estate that pairs the Golf GTI's engine with a 640-litre boot. Now a unique proposition among mainstream brands, effective and practical, but expensive, with a DSG gearbox that is sluggish in normal driving.
m: DSG7 gearbox sluggish in D mode
Sharply higher price, options and French malus tax
Skoda|Octavia Combi RS.q: Families wanting a fast, discreet estate
Skoda|Octavia Combi RS.s: The 2024 facelift raised power to 265 hp. The diesel, plug-in hybrid and 4x4 RS versions have gone: only this petrol version remains.

Skoda|Octavia RS.v: A versatile sporting saloon that uses the Golf GTI's engine with a family-car boot. Fast and effective, it is less playful than a Golf GTI and its price has risen sharply.
m: Sharply higher price and French malus tax
Skoda|Octavia RS.q: Drivers wanting a discreet, practical performance car
Skoda|Octavia RS.s: The 2024 facelift raised power to 265 hp (+20 hp). It shares its engine with the VW Golf GTI. The diesel RS has gone.

Skoda|Peaq.v: A large electric family SUV that focuses on comfort, refinement and interior space, with solid range. Rapid charging capped at 200 kW and a bill quickly inflated by options temper the verdict.
p: Spacious cabin, large boot as a 5-seater
m: Charging limited to 200 kW and 11 kW AC
Skoda|Peaq.q: Large families looking for a comfortable electric SUV for long journeys
Skoda|Peaq.s: Skoda's largest electric model (4.87 m long, 2.97 m wheelbase), it charges from 10-80% in 28 minutes and offers V2L. The third row is better suited to children or shorter adults according to What Car?.
Skoda|Peaq.x: Tests mainly cover the 4x4 “Battery 90x 299 hp”, often in Sportline trim with adaptive suspension; Mac4Ever also drove the “Battery 90 286 hp”. Top Gear recommends this rear-wheel-drive version, which goes further, and reserves the 4x4 for snow or towing.

Skoda|Scala.v: A hatchback offering very good space for the money, with a large boot and a comfortable ride. Rational but bland, it remains a cheaper alternative to the Peugeot 308 or Volkswagen Golf.
m: Wind and road noise on the motorway
Skoda|Scala.q: Sensible buyers wanting space at a fair price
Skoda|Scala.s: Facelifted in 2024 like the Kamiq, it sits on the Fabia's MQB-A0 platform, not the Golf's MQB base.

Skoda|Superb.v: A large, spacious, quiet and very well-built hatchback saloon, a rare breed on today's market. A rational alternative to German premium saloons, more convincing as a diesel than with the 1.5 TSI.
m: 1.5 TSI mild hybrid a little underpowered
Prices up sharply on this generation
Skoda|Superb.q: Executives or families wanting a large, comfortable saloon
Skoda|Superb.s: Co-developed with the VW Passat, which is now only sold as an estate: the Superb hatchback has no Volkswagen twin.
Skoda|Superb.x: The 2.0 TDI 150 hp is judged the best compromise, frugal and punchier; the 1.5 TSI Hybrid 150 hp feels underpowered for a car this size, and its DSG gearbox can be hesitant.

Skoda|Superb Combi.v: A large estate with a class-leading boot, comfortable and well thought out. Co-developed with the VW Passat, it rivals German premium estates for space, but its entry price is high.
m: DSG gearbox slow to respond when driven briskly
Skoda|Superb Combi.q: High-mileage drivers or families needing space
Skoda|Superb Combi.s: Built in Bratislava on the same base as the VW Passat. The plug-in hybrid claims more than 100 km of range and supports rapid charging.
Skoda|Superb Combi.x: The 2.0 TDI 150 hp, livelier and more frugal, is preferred to the 1.5 TSI Hybrid 150 hp; the plug-in hybrid loses out on comfort with its 19-inch wheels and extra weight.

Smart|#1.v: The #1 impresses with its interior space, careful presentation and generous equipment. The Brabus delivers lively performance but uses considerably more energy than the rear-wheel-drive version.
p: Roomy rear seats, sliding rear bench
Good sound insulation and comfortable seats
m: Boot on the small side for the class
High consumption of the Brabus version
Rear access hampered by the roofline
Smart|#1.q: Well-off city dwellers wanting a roomy, well-equipped electric compact SUV
Smart|#1.s: AC charging goes up to 22 kW on the best-equipped versions, a rare asset in the class, compared with 7.4 kW on the entry-level model.
Smart|#1.x: The rear-wheel-drive 62 kWh 272 hp proved frugal in Motor1's test; the Brabus 428 hp, lively with plenty of traction, uses considerably more energy and its damping divides opinion.

Smart|#3.v: Roomier than the #1, the #3 offers excellent value for its equipment and is pleasant to drive. Its intrusive warning chimes and all-touchscreen ergonomics grate in daily use.
p: Generous rear space for its size
Good build quality and sound insulation
Smart|#3.q: Couples or small families looking for a well-equipped electric coupé-SUV
Smart|#3.s: Built in China, the #3 is no longer eligible for the French EV incentive.
Smart|#3.x: The rear-wheel-drive 62 kWh 272 hp proved frugal and enjoyable to drive; the Brabus 428 hp has impressive acceleration, but its sport mode and chassis divide the press.

Smart|#5.v: Spacious, comfortable and well built, the #5 takes on the best electric family SUVs and charges very quickly. High consumption and invasive alerts take some of the shine off.
p: Very generous cabin space and boot
Comfort, sound insulation and build quality
Very fast charging on high-power chargers
m: Overly intrusive alerts and driver aids
Smart|#5.q: Families wanting a large, roomy electric SUV that charges quickly
Smart|#5.s: Built in China, the #5 gets no French EV incentive and is subject to EU import duties.
Smart|#5.x: L'argus rates the rear-wheel-drive 94 kWh 363 hp as highly recommendable. The Brabus 646 hp, with blistering acceleration, is judged too expensive and needlessly powerful there, but well positioned according to Automobile Propre.

Suzuki|Across.v: A clone of the Toyota RAV4 plug-in hybrid, the Across offers strong performance, useful electric range and generous equipment. It is nonetheless expensive for a Suzuki and nearing the end of its life.
p: Electric range useful day to day
m: Boot space eaten into by the battery
Suzuki|Across.q: Families who drive mostly on electric day to day and occasionally travel further
Suzuki|Across.s: A new generation, still derived from the Toyota RAV4, has been announced to replace this model in France.

Suzuki|S-Cross.v: A rational, frugal and very well-equipped SUV, the S-Cross offers AllGrip all-wheel drive at a reasonable price. Its dated cabin and uninspiring handling leave it behind the class leaders.
p: Controlled consumption with the 1.4 mild hybrid
m: Dated cabin carried over from the old model
Vague steering and pronounced body roll
Suzuki|S-Cross.q: Rural families looking for a simple all-wheel-drive SUV
Suzuki|S-Cross.s: Suzuki warranty of 3 years or 100,000 km, extendable to 10 years or 200,000 km with annual servicing and checks at the dealer network.
Suzuki|S-Cross.x: AllGrip all-wheel drive, effective on slippery surfaces, is recommended if the budget allows; the economical automatic gearbox sometimes changes up too early.

Suzuki|Swace.v: Suzuki's version of the Toyota Corolla Touring Sports, the Swace shares its economy and large load space, but also its lack of dynamism. Its end of production was announced for 2025.
m: Only one engine, without Toyota's 2.0 hybrid
Small battery, very limited electric mode
Suzuki|Swace.q: Families or high-mileage drivers looking for an economical hybrid estate
Suzuki|Swace.s: Built by Toyota in the UK (Burnaston), with production announced to end in 2025: check availability with dealers.

Suzuki|Swift.v: The Swift relies on lightness and economy with a three-cylinder mild-hybrid engine. Agile, economical and well equipped, it is short on power and its build quality feels cheap.
p: 4x4 AllGrip version, rare in a city car
Suzuki|Swift.q: Buyers on a small budget looking for a frugal, easy-going city car
Suzuki|Swift.s: Suzuki warranty of 3 years or 100,000 km, extendable to 10 years or 200,000 km with annual servicing and checks at the dealer network.
Suzuki|Swift.x: The 1.2 Hybrid Manual, with its short, precise gearbox, is the most recommended; the Auto (CVT) is judged less pleasant, while the AllGrip adds weight and uses more fuel.

Suzuki|Vitara.v: Launched in 2015 and facelifted in 2024, the Vitara shows its age inside, but remains comfortable and frugal and offers AllGrip all-wheel drive, chosen by around 40% of French buyers.
p: More enjoyable to drive than expected
m: Firm suspension on poor road surfaces
Suzuki|Vitara.q: Rural or mountain dwellers wanting an affordable compact 4x4
Suzuki|Vitara.s: Suzuki warranty of 3 years or 100,000 km, extendable to 10 years or 200,000 km with annual servicing and checks at the dealer network.

Suzuki|e Vitara.v: Suzuki's first electric SUV, the e Vitara stands out with AllGrip-e all-wheel drive, rare in its class. Simple and backed by a good warranty, it falls down on a tight boot and high consumption.
p: Interior space and sliding rear bench
Suzuki|e Vitara.q: Rural drivers looking for an all-wheel-drive electric SUV
Suzuki|e Vitara.s: Built in India, it shares its platform with the Toyota Urban Cruiser. LFP battery supplied by BYD; Suzuki warranty extendable to 10 years with servicing at the dealer network.
Suzuki|e Vitara.x: The 144 hp is enough in town and the suburbs; the 174 hp gains range and power; the AllGrip-e 183 hp adds traction on slippery surfaces at the cost of a smaller boot and reduced range.

Tesla|Model 3.v: A very efficient and agile electric saloon, backed by the Supercharger network. The all-screen ergonomics and steering-wheel indicator buttons grate, and the driver aids lag behind.
m: Almost all controls on the screen
Indicator buttons on the steering wheel
Tesla|Model 3.q: High-mileage drivers wanting an efficient electric saloon
Tesla|Model 3.s: Facelifted in late 2023 (“Highland” project): revised suspension and sound insulation, ventilated front seats and an 8-inch rear screen.
Tesla|Model 3.x: The RWD 282 hp is the most frugal; the Long Range AWD 440 hp, with more range, offers welcome traction in rain and snow.

Tesla|Model Y.v: A very roomy and efficient electric SUV, the Model Y facelifted in 2025 gains in comfort and build quality. The Supercharger network remains an asset; suspension still firm over small bumps is a drawback.
m: Suspension still firm at low speed
Everything on the screen, no CarPlay or Android Auto
Tesla|Model Y.q: Families wanting a roomy electric SUV for travelling
Tesla|Model Y.s: A stripped-back Standard version (cloth upholstery, covered glass roof, no rear screen) has been sold in France since late 2025.
Tesla|Model Y.x: The Long Range RWD 300 hp is judged the most sensible choice for its price and range; the AWD 351 hp adds liveliness and traction on wet roads.

Toyota|Aygo X.v: Now a hybrid, the Aygo X is much livelier and very frugal, without losing its urban agility. But rear space and boot remain very tight, and the firm suspension makes itself felt on fast roads.
p: Very low consumption, a hybrid unique in the A segment
Agile and easy to manoeuvre in town
Much better performance than the old 1.0
m: Very limited rear space and boot
Firm suspension, wind noise on the motorway
Pricier than the Hyundai i10 or Kia Picanto
Toyota|Aygo X.q: City dwellers who drive mostly in town and want minimal consumption
Toyota|Aygo X.s: Named “Small Car of the Year 2026” by the British magazine What Car? The 1.5 hybrid replaces the old 1.0 three-cylinder petrol.

Toyota|C-HR.v: The second-generation C-HR banks on very bold styling and a frugal hybrid range, including a plug-in. But the rear seats remain dark and cramped, and the boot is tight, especially in the plug-in.
m: Small boot, especially in the plug-in hybrid
Toyota|C-HR.q: Couples or small families won over by the styling and economy
Toyota|C-HR.s: Toyota Relax warranty of up to 10 years or 185,000 km, renewed at each service at the Toyota network.
Toyota|C-HR.x: The 1.8 Hybrid 140 hp is enough in town and the suburbs but struggles on hills; the 2.0 hybrid is more at ease on the open road. The 223 hp plug-in, lively and smooth, loses boot space and costs more.

Toyota|C-HR+.v: More convincing than Toyota's first EVs, the C-HR+ wins people over with its efficiency, comfort and equipment. Boot, rear visibility and storage lag behind its rivals.
p: Generous equipment from the entry-level trim
m: Little regeneration adjustment, no one-pedal mode
Toyota|C-HR+.q: Drivers who put efficiency and comfort ahead of boot space
Toyota|C-HR+.s: Built in Japan (Toyota City), it is not eligible for the French EV incentive. Battery guaranteed for up to 10 years or 1 million km, subject to servicing at the dealer network.
Toyota|C-HR+.x: The Long Range 224 hp, the most widely tested, offers the best compromise; it's best to stick with the 18-inch wheels, as the 20-inch ones reduce range.

Toyota|Corolla.v: The Corolla hybrid stands out for its economy and much-improved drivability since the 2023 update. It falls behind on rear space and boot, especially with the 2.0.
m: Boot reduced by the hybrid system, especially the 2.0
Toyota|Corolla.q: Drivers who prioritise economy and peace of mind
Toyota|Corolla.s: Toyota Relax warranty of up to 10 years or 185,000 km, renewed at each service at the Toyota network.
Toyota|Corolla.x: The 1.8 Hybrid 140 hp, the most frugal, is enough for most uses; the 2.0 Hybrid 178 hp, much livelier, suits more demanding drivers but cuts boot space further.

Toyota|Corolla Touring.v: The Corolla estate combines the economy of Toyota's hybrid with smooth, relaxing driving. An economical family car but not much fun to drive, and noisy under hard acceleration.
Toyota|Corolla Touring.q: Families or high-mileage drivers looking for a reliable hybrid estate
Toyota|Corolla Touring.s: Built in the UK. Toyota Relax warranty of up to 10 years or 185,000 km, renewed at each service at the Toyota network.
Toyota|Corolla Touring.x: The 1.8 Hybrid 140 hp is enough for relaxed driving and costs less; the 2.0 Hybrid 178 hp, livelier and less strained on the motorway, has a slightly smaller boot.

Toyota|GR Supra.v: Developed with BMW, the GR Supra offers a punchy straight-six and an optional manual gearbox. An effective but cramped coupé, now at the end of its life.
Toyota|GR Supra.s: Production ended in March 2026 with no successor announced: availability limited to stock. Built in Austria alongside the BMW Z4.

Toyota|GR Yaris.v: Updated in 2024, the GR Yaris gains 20 hp, a lower driving position and a convincing automatic gearbox, without losing any of its driving fun. Its price has, however, risen sharply.
Toyota|GR Yaris.q: Driving enthusiasts wanting a car for fun
Toyota|GR Yaris.s: Updated in 2024: power raised to 280 hp and a new eight-speed Aisin automatic gearbox, alongside the six-speed manual.
Toyota|GR Yaris.x: The 1.6 GR Manual remains the most engaging and the most in demand; the 1.6 GR Auto, quick and well geared, makes everyday use easier without betraying the car's character.

Toyota|Land Cruiser.v: The Land Cruiser remains a genuine body-on-frame off-roader, highly capable off road and fit for heavy towing. On the road it is heavy and clumsy, its diesel is rough and its price high.
Toyota|Land Cruiser.q: Buyers with genuine off-road or towing needs
Toyota|Land Cruiser.s: At almost 280 g/km of CO2 (WLTP), this diesel is hit hard by the French malus tax.

Toyota|Mirai.v: A quiet, technically accomplished hydrogen saloon, the Mirai refuels in a few minutes. But the very sparse station network, the cost of hydrogen and limited interior space make it one for fleets.
Toyota|Mirai.q: Fleets or taxis with a hydrogen station nearby
Toyota|Mirai.s: The rear bench does not fold, and the central tunnel housing a hydrogen tank makes the middle rear seat uncomfortable.

Toyota|Prius.v: The fifth-generation Prius breaks with its image thanks to a low-slung shape and a powerful plug-in hybrid. Frugal and pleasant to drive, it sacrifices rear space, boot and visibility.
Toyota|Prius.q: Design-conscious drivers who can charge often
Toyota|Prius.s: In Europe, the Prius is only offered as a plug-in hybrid. Toyota Relax warranty of up to 10 years or 185,000 km, renewed at each service.

Toyota|RAV4.v: The sixth-generation RAV4 remains a well-rounded, comfortable and roomy hybrid SUV that trades on Toyota's reliability. Lacklustre drivability, less flattering build quality and high prices dampen its appeal.
p: Generous equipment from the entry-level trim
m: Unpleasant CVT gearbox and front end
High prices, heavy French malus tax on the plug-in
Toyota|RAV4.q: Families who put reliability and comfort ahead of driving enjoyment
Toyota|RAV4.s: Built in Japan for Europe. 3-year or 100,000 km warranty, extended to 5 years for the hybrid system and its battery.
Toyota|RAV4.x: The 2.5 Hybrid 2WD 185 hp is the most sensible choice; the AWD-i 194 hp, barely livelier, is heavier and more heavily taxed. The Plug-in Hybrid AWD-i 309 hp, far quicker, is hit by a heavy weight-based malus.

Toyota|Yaris.v: Now with 130 hp, the Yaris hybrid remains a benchmark for economy in town. But rear space and boot are limited, the engine is audible under acceleration and prices are high.
Toyota|Yaris.q: City dwellers wanting a frugal hybrid that needs no charging
Toyota|Yaris.s: Built notably near Valenciennes. Toyota Relax warranty of up to 10 years or 185,000 km, renewed at each service at the Toyota network.
Toyota|Yaris.x: The 1.5 Hybrid 130 hp, more responsive in town and when accelerating, uses barely more than the 116 hp, but gets noisier when pushed and costs considerably more.

Toyota|Yaris Cross.v: The Yaris Cross combines Toyota's frugal hybrid with compact dimensions and optional all-wheel drive. A lacklustre interior, firm suspension in town and tight rear seats count against it.
p: Easy to drive, improved sound insulation
Toyota|Yaris Cross.q: Urban drivers looking for a frugal compact SUV
Toyota|Yaris Cross.s: Built in France, at Onnaing near Valenciennes, on the same line as the Yaris. Toyota Relax warranty of up to 10 years or 185,000 km, renewed at each service.
Toyota|Yaris Cross.x: The 1.5 Hybrid 130 hp uses as much as the 116 hp for a little more liveliness; the 1.5 Hybrid 4x4 130 hp, slower and thirstier, also has a smaller boot.

Toyota|bZ4x.v: Extensively revised in 2025, the bZ4X gains in efficiency, range and quietness. A rational, competent but unexciting electric SUV, held back by a boot smaller than its rivals' and an austere interface.
m: Austere interface with sometimes confusing menus
Toyota|bZ4x.q: Families wanting a comfortable, rational electric SUV
Toyota|bZ4x.s: The 2025 facelift brings 10-80% rapid charging in around thirty minutes and a 22 kW on-board charger on higher trims.
Toyota|bZ4x.x: The Long Range 224 hp offers the best balance; the Performance AWD 343 hp, much quicker, uses considerably more energy and can tow up to 1,500 kg.

Toyota|bZ4x Touring.v: A raised estate version of the bZ4X, the Touring wins people over with its generous boot, rear space and comfort. Range and charging remain average, and the interior has changed little.
p: Very roomy boot, among the largest
Good balance between comfort and handling
m: Range and charging outdone by rivals
Hard plastics in the boot, fixed rear bench
Toyota|bZ4x Touring.q: Active families looking for a roomy EV, possibly with 4x4
Toyota|bZ4x Touring.s: Battery guaranteed for up to 10 years or 1 million km (70% capacity), subject to an annual check at the Toyota network.
Toyota|bZ4x Touring.x: The Long Range 224 hp, more efficient, is enough for most uses; the Performance AWD 380 hp, very lively and able to tow 1,500 kg, uses more energy and rides more firmly.

Volkswagen|Golf.v: The Golf remains a benchmark for its balance of comfort, build quality and versatility. The 2024 facelift addressed some of the criticism of its ergonomics, but it lacks emotion and comes at a high price.
m: Annoying engine cut-outs in the mild hybrid
Volkswagen|Golf.q: Drivers wanting a versatile, well-engineered hatchback
Volkswagen|Golf.s: Facelifted in 2024: faster MIB4 infotainment on a 12.9-inch screen and the return of real buttons on the steering wheel, across all trims.
Volkswagen|Golf.x: The 1.5 eTSI Hybrid 116 hp, refined but prone to engine cut-outs, is the rational choice in the range; the 1.5 eTSI Hybrid 150 hp is smoother and punchier with the DSG7 gearbox.

Volkswagen|Golf SW.v: The Golf estate is an accomplished, well-rounded family car, roomy and smooth to drive, with ergonomics simplified since 2024. It still offers a diesel, now a rarity, but is pricey against its rivals.
Volkswagen|Golf SW.q: High-mileage drivers or families wanting a roomy compact estate
Volkswagen|Golf SW.s: Its technical cousin, the slightly longer Skoda Octavia Combi, offers comparable quality for less money.
Volkswagen|Golf SW.x: The 1.5 eTSI Hybrid 150 hp, smooth and efficient, is the recommended choice; the 2.0 TDIs only make sense for high-mileage motorway drivers.

Volkswagen|ID. Cross.v: Tested in prototype form, the ID. Cross is a practical, comfortable small electric SUV that brings back physical buttons. Uninspiring to drive, it fixes the flaws of the early ID models.
m: Regeneration setting buried in the menus
High rear floor for tall passengers
Volkswagen|ID. Cross.q: City dwellers or small families wanting a practical compact electric SUV
Volkswagen|ID. Cross.s: It shares its platform and powertrains with the Skoda Epiq. Published tests are of advanced prototypes in 52 kWh 211 hp form.

Volkswagen|ID. Polo.v: The ID. Polo is a roomy, efficient electric city car that charges quickly, with a reassuring chassis. A little harsh on 19-inch wheels, it becomes pricier than a Renault 5 from the mid-range trims upwards.
m: Harsh over small bumps on 19-inch wheels
Pricier than a Renault 5 in mid-range trims
Hard plastics, wind and road noise
Volkswagen|ID. Polo.q: City dwellers or small families wanting a versatile, roomy EV
Volkswagen|ID. Polo.s: Built in Spain (Martorell). LFP battery on the 37 kWh versions, NMC on the 52 kWh; the heat pump remains a paid option on all trims.
Volkswagen|ID. Polo.x: The 37 kWh versions (116 and 135 hp) are enough in town and match the Renault 5 on price; the 52 kWh 211 hp, livelier and with more range, charges quickly but costs considerably more.

Volkswagen|ID. Tiguan.v: Replacing the ID.4, the ID. Tiguan gains in quietness, comfort and ease of use. Its rapid charging remains average and its driving bland; the first tests are of prototypes.
p: Quieter and more comfortable than the ID.4
Roomy cabin and small front boot (frunk)
m: Evolution rather than revolution over the ID.4
Volkswagen|ID. Tiguan.q: Families wanting a comfortable, easy-to-use electric SUV
Volkswagen|ID. Tiguan.s: Verdict based on short drives in camouflaged prototypes, ahead of the official unveiling in October 2026. Production planned at Emden, Germany.
Volkswagen|ID. Tiguan.x: The 58 kWh, with an LFP battery reputed to be more durable, accepts lower charging power than the 77 kWh; the prototype drives don't yet separate the versions on the road.

Volkswagen|ID.3.v: An agile electric hatchback, roomy thanks to its rear-wheel-drive layout, the ID.3 had its interior upgraded in 2023, but its touch-based ergonomics are still criticised. The facelifted 2026 Neo version fixes the essentials.
p: Solid range with the large battery
m: Tesla and MG4 more aggressive on price
Volkswagen|ID.3.q: Drivers ready for electric looking for a roomy hatchback
Volkswagen|ID.3.s: Facelifted in 2026 as the ID.3 Neo: revised dashboard, real steering-wheel buttons, One Pedal mode and V2L.

Volkswagen|ID.3 Neo.v: The ID.3's second facelift, the Neo finally fixes its ergonomics with a classier interior and the return of physical buttons. Frugal, roomy and pleasant to drive, it remains pricier than its rivals.
m: Pricier than the Mégane, MG4 or Leapmotor B03
Volkswagen|ID.3 Neo.q: Drivers ready for electric looking for a roomy, efficient hatchback
Volkswagen|ID.3 Neo.s: With a qualifying French eco-score, it is eligible for the CEE-funded French EV incentive. The 79 kWh 231 hp costs almost €3,000 more than the equivalent old ID.3.

Volkswagen|ID.4.v: A comfortable, quiet and roomy electric SUV, the ID.4 gained power and better ergonomics with its mid-life update. It remains less efficient and slower to charge than the best rivals.
Volkswagen|ID.4.q: Families switching to electric who prioritise comfort
Volkswagen|ID.4.s: Its mid-life update brought a 286 hp rear motor, a 12.9-inch central screen and a revised, more responsive interface.

Volkswagen|ID.5.v: The coupé version of the ID.4, the ID.5 sharpens the styling while keeping a spacious cabin and a large boot. It costs more than its cousin, however, without being more enjoyable to drive, GTX aside.
m: Pricier than the ID.4 with no extra space
Volkswagen|ID.5.q: Drivers wanting an electric family SUV with bolder styling
Volkswagen|ID.5.s: It shares its platform, cabin and powertrains with the ID.4; its boot (549 litres) is even slightly larger, but a little less tall.
Volkswagen|ID.5.x: Only the all-wheel-drive GTX 340 hp is more dynamic than an ID.4; the rear-wheel-drive Pro 286 hp drives just like it, for a lower price.

Volkswagen|ID.7.v: A comfortable and quiet large electric saloon, the ID.7 stands out for its class-leading range and spacious cabin. It remains expensive, uninvolving to drive, and its touch controls grate.
Volkswagen|ID.7.q: High-mileage drivers wanting an electric saloon for long journeys
Volkswagen|ID.7.s: A direct rival to the Tesla Model 3 and Hyundai Ioniq 6, it is also available as an estate (ID.7 Tourer).
Volkswagen|ID.7.x: The Pro 286 hp (77 kWh) is judged the best buy; the pricier Pro S only makes sense if you really need the extra range of its 86 kWh battery.

Volkswagen|ID.7 Tourer.v: Volkswagen's electric estate combines a very large boot, top-class comfort and long range. A rare and accomplished package, but the GTX carries a hefty premium for minimal extra dynamism.
m: Air vents and settings relegated to the touchscreen
Volkswagen|ID.7 Tourer.q: Families or professionals wanting an electric estate for travelling
Volkswagen|ID.7 Tourer.s: One of the few fully electric estates; its 605-litre boot beats that of the BMW i5 Touring, a more upmarket rival like the Audi A6 Avant e-tron.
Volkswagen|ID.7 Tourer.x: The Pro S, with the large battery, is judged the best choice for a small premium over the Pro; the GTX 340 hp, pricier, firmer and with less range, adds little in driving enjoyment.

Volkswagen|Passat.v: Now offered only as an estate, the ninth-generation Passat is a comfortable, quiet and very spacious long-distance cruiser, a solid alternative to SUVs. Its size, touch controls and costly options hold it back.
p: Plug-in hybrid with long electric range
Volkswagen|Passat.q: High-mileage drivers or families wanting a large, comfortable estate
Volkswagen|Passat.s: Developed with Skoda, it comes off the same line as its technical twin the Skoda Superb, sharing everything down to the umbrella stored in the door.

Volkswagen|Polo.v: A serious, well-built city car that is pleasant on the road, playing the maturity card rather than boldness. Its price remains high for the class and the range is limited to non-hybrid petrol engines.
p: Solid build quality for the class
207 hp GTI at the top of the range
Volkswagen|Polo.q: Drivers wanting a versatile, reassuring city car without electrification
Volkswagen|Polo.s: Built in South Africa since 2024, it is sold alongside the electric ID. Polo, in showrooms since September 2026.

Volkswagen|T-Cross.v: A small SUV made practical by its sliding rear bench and versatile boot, sound and comfortable. The 2024 facelift improves interior quality; the lack of a hybrid and the prices of higher trims weigh against it.
Volkswagen|T-Cross.q: Urban families wanting a practical, easy-going small SUV
Volkswagen|T-Cross.s: Facelifted in 2024: subtle styling tweaks, matrix headlights on higher trims and a soft-touch dashboard.
Volkswagen|T-Cross.x: The 1.0 TSI 95 hp lacks puff; the 116 hp, manual or DSG7, is judged the best compromise, with the quieter 1.5 TSI DSG7 150 hp not adding enough to justify its extra cost.

Volkswagen|T-Roc.v: Longer and better built, the new T-Roc improves in comfort, rear space and boot capacity. It drops the diesel, and prices climb quickly with options.
p: Higher perceived quality, fabric on the dashboard
Volkswagen|T-Roc.q: Buyers wanting a versatile compact SUV better built than the old one
Volkswagen|T-Roc.s: All versions are electrified, as 48V mild hybrids or full hybrids; a sporty R version is due to join the range later.
Volkswagen|T-Roc.x: The 1.5 eTSI Hybrid 116 hp is adequate despite the extra weight; the 150 hp, much livelier with no extra consumption, is the only one to get adaptive dampers in R-Line trim.

Volkswagen|T-Roc Cabriolet.v: One of the market's rare convertible SUVs, the T-Roc Cabriolet offers open-top driving without sacrificing everyday usability. Its price is high and both boot and rear space are limited.
p: Only convertible SUV in its class
m: End of the line with no successor
Volkswagen|T-Roc Cabriolet.q: Open-top fans who want to keep a high driving position
Volkswagen|T-Roc Cabriolet.s: Volkswagen has announced it is dropping convertibles: the T-Roc Cabriolet, based on the previous generation, will not be replaced.

Volkswagen|Taigo.v: The coupé version of the T-Cross, the Taigo puts style first while remaining pleasant to drive and roomy. The sloping rear window hampers rear visibility, and both materials and prices are a little disappointing.
Volkswagen|Taigo.q: Style-conscious buyers wanting a different kind of small SUV
Volkswagen|Taigo.s: It uses the T-Cross platform, but without its sliding rear bench; boot capacity is similar, with a high load sill.

Volkswagen|Tayron.v: Successor to the Tiguan Allspace, the Tayron offers vast space, good comfort and sound insulation, and a plug-in hybrid with long electric range. Uninspiring to drive, it costs more than its mainstream rivals.
p: Plug-in hybrid with long electric range
m: Seven seats unavailable on the plug-in hybrid
Volkswagen|Tayron.q: Large families wanting a big, roomy and comfortable SUV
Volkswagen|Tayron.s: It replaces the Tiguan Allspace. DCC adaptive dampers are deemed key to comfort, which suffers on the R-Line's 20-inch wheels.
Volkswagen|Tayron.x: The 2.0 TDI Auto 150 hp suits high-mileage drivers and towing; the smoother eHybrid makes sense with home charging, but only as a five-seater; the 1.5 eTSI 150 hp has to be worked hard.

Volkswagen|Tiguan.v: The third-generation Tiguan improves in comfort, presentation and ergonomics. Its plug-in hybrid claims more than 100 km of electric range, but prices have risen sharply.
p: Plug-in hybrid with long electric range
m: Smaller boot on the plug-in hybrid
Limited traction on wet roads (272 hp)
Volkswagen|Tiguan.q: Families wanting a versatile, comfortable and well-equipped SUV
Volkswagen|Tiguan.s: The plug-in hybrid now supports rapid charging at up to 50 kW, but its boot loses around 160 litres compared with the combustion versions.
Volkswagen|Tiguan.x: The cheaper eHybrid 204 hp is judged just as sensible as the 272 hp, whose traction is caught out on wet roads; once the French malus tax is included, it costs as much as the diesel.

Volkswagen|Touareg.v: A large status SUV, the Touareg combines fine build quality, top-class comfort and high power in plug-in hybrid form. Its price pits it against premium SUVs.
Volkswagen|Touareg.q: Demanding drivers wanting a large, upmarket and powerful SUV
Volkswagen|Touareg.s: Production ended in March 2026 after a 24-year career, with no direct successor announced.

Volkswagen|Touran.v: One of the last true compact MPVs, the Touran remains very practical with its individual rear seats. Its design dates back to 2015 and production has ended.
Volkswagen|Touran.q: Large families who put space and versatility ahead of style
Volkswagen|Touran.s: Production ended at Wolfsburg at the end of April 2026, with no direct successor: only stock vehicles remain.

Volvo|EC40.v: The coupé version of the EX40, trading space and visibility for a sleeker silhouette. Build quality, quietness and performance appeal, but the price remains high and the infotainment is ageing.
p: Lively performance, blistering in Twin form
Volvo|EC40.q: Premium buyers who put style ahead of space
Volvo|EC40.s: It was called the C40 Recharge before being renamed. Rivals: Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron and BMW iX2. Its Google-based infotainment does not offer Android Auto.
Volvo|EC40.x: The Single Extended Range 252 hp is judged the best choice, with more range than the Single for a small premium; the Twin Performance 442 hp, with blistering acceleration, costs considerably more.

Volvo|ES90.v: A large, quiet, comfortable and well-finished electric saloon that charges quickly thanks to its 800V architecture. Limited rear visibility, overly touch-based ergonomics and limited manoeuvrability are its flaws.
Volvo|ES90.q: High-mileage drivers wanting a large, comfortable electric saloon
Volvo|ES90.s: Air suspension standard only on the Ultra trim. No estate version. Rivals: BMW i5, Audi A6 e-tron, Mercedes EQE.
Volvo|ES90.x: Only the Single Extended Range 333 hp has been tested: judged lively enough, it is the press's pick. The more powerful Twin versions have a bigger battery and slightly faster charging.

Volvo|EX30.v: Volvo's smallest SUV, lively, comfortable and manoeuvrable in town. Its all-screen ergonomics with no instrument display in front of the driver, tight rear seats and build quality below the brand's usual standard divide opinion.
m: All controls grouped on the screen
Volvo|EX30.q: Well-off city dwellers wanting a premium small electric SUV
Volvo|EX30.s: Battery guaranteed for 8 years or 160,000 km. A raised Cross Country version is offered only as the P8 AWD.
Volvo|EX30.x: The P5 Long Range is the best balanced; the small-battery P5 mainly suits town use, and the P8 AWD, judged overpowered, mostly makes sense for winters in the mountains.

Volvo|EX40.v: The electric version of the XC40, well built, comfortable and very fast in Twin Performance form. It remains expensive for a compact SUV and its real-world range falls short of the official figures.
m: Cabin not upmarket enough for the price
Volvo|EX40.q: Drivers wanting a compact electric SUV with premium comfort
Volvo|EX40.s: Formerly the XC40 Recharge, renamed in 2024. It keeps a more conventional interface than the EX30 and EX90, which put almost everything on the screen.
Volvo|EX40.x: The Single versions, with softer suspension, make good family cars; the Twin Performance, very fast and well balanced, strays further from its official range.

Volvo|EX60.v: An electric family SUV that debuts Volvo's 800V SPA3 platform. First-rate range and charging, remarkable comfort and quietness, for a drive that is more serene than engaging.
m: Controls heavily reliant on the screen
Pricier and shorter-ranged than a BMW iX3
Volvo|EX60.q: High-mileage families wanting a long-range premium EV
Volvo|EX60.s: It debuts the SPA3 platform: battery integrated into the body structure and large castings. Battery guaranteed for 8 years or 160,000 km. Rivals: BMW iX3, Mercedes GLC.
Volvo|EX60.x: The rear-wheel-drive P6 is the most agile; the P10 AWD accelerates harder but loses a little bite. The P12, the only one with the large battery, has not yet been tested.

Volvo|EX90.v: A large, comfortable, quiet and well-finished seven-seat electric SUV. Its all-touch ergonomics make it hard to get to grips with, and its 400V charging seems dated at this price.
Volvo|EX90.q: Well-off large families wanting a premium seven-seat electric SUV
Volvo|EX90.s: Arrived in late 2024 almost two years behind schedule, with software still being finalised. Third row mainly suited to children. It is sold alongside the hybrid XC90.
Volvo|EX90.x: The Twin (408 hp when tested, now 456 hp) is more than enough, provided you engage “Constant 4WD” mode for sharper responses; the Twin Performance only adds extra punch of little use. The Single has not been tested.

Volvo|V60.v: An elegant, comfortable and practical premium estate that favours serenity over dynamism. Its technology is starting to show its age, and the plug-in hybrid only makes sense with home charging.
p: Elegant lines that are ageing well
m: Dated infotainment, climate controls in the screen
Volvo|V60.q: Drivers who prefer a premium estate to an SUV
Volvo|V60.s: On the plug-in hybrid, the battery reduces boot space by around 50 litres. Rivals: BMW 3 Series Touring, Mercedes C-Class Estate, Audi A5 Avant.
Volvo|V60.x: The more affordable B4 mild hybrid is enough for touring; the T6 plug-in hybrid, livelier and frugal day to day if kept charged, loses boot space and costs considerably more.

Volvo|XC40.v: A comfortable, practical and well-finished premium compact SUV, the XC40 is now only offered as a petrol mild hybrid, with no full or plug-in hybrid. Its consumption, higher than its rivals', counts against it.
p: Fine build quality and interior design
Practical cabin with plenty of storage
Comfort and quietness on the motorway
m: Rear seats and boot a little tight
Controls too reliant on the screen
Volvo|XC40.q: Drivers wanting a premium compact combustion SUV with no need to charge
Volvo|XC40.s: Lightly facelifted in 2022. Its electric version, formerly the XC40 Recharge, has been sold as the EX40 since 2024.
Volvo|XC40.x: The B4 is about a second quicker from 0-100 km/h than the B3, at the cost of slightly higher consumption.

Volvo|XC60.v: An elegant and relaxing premium family SUV, now the best-selling model in Volvo's history. Its plug-in hybrid versions are powerful, but expensive and thirsty with a flat battery.
m: High consumption with a flat battery
Volvo|XC60.q: Well-off families wanting a comfortable SUV who can charge at home
Volvo|XC60.s: Facelifted in 2025: 11.2-inch central screen and more responsive infotainment. No rapid charging. Rivals: Audi Q5, BMW X3, Mercedes GLC.

Volvo|XC90.v: A large, comfortable and luxurious seven-seat family SUV, facelifted in late 2024. Its design dates back to 2015, its real-world electric range disappoints and its price, with options, is very high.
p: Seven seats and great comfort on the road
Volvo|XC90.q: Well-off large families wanting a seven-seat plug-in hybrid SUV
Volvo|XC90.s: Facelifted in late 2024 (11.2-inch central screen), it is sold alongside the EX90, its fully electric equivalent.

XPeng|G6.v: A roomy, well-equipped family SUV, among the fastest-charging on the market, especially since its facelift. Firm suspension, intrusive driver aids and all-touch ergonomics temper the verdict.
p: Rapid charging among the best on the market
Generous standard equipment for the price
m: Firm suspension, especially at low speed
Almost all controls on the central screen
XPeng|G6.q: Families who make long journeys and want to charge quickly
XPeng|G6.s: The facelift swapped the NMC battery for an LFP one: charging is faster, but the car gains around 100 kg and loses a little WLTP range.

XPeng|G9.v: A large, very roomy and well-finished SUV that charges quickly. Unconvincing handling, hesitant driver aids and a confusing touch interface leave it behind at this price point.
m: Poorly controlled and sometimes harsh suspension
Slow central screen with confusing menus
XPeng|G9.q: Families who prioritise cabin space and long journeys
XPeng|G9.s: Founded in 2014, Xpeng is still little known in France: its network had only 15 dealerships at the time of L'argus's test in September 2024.

XPeng|P7+.v: A large, comfortable, well-equipped electric saloon that is among the fastest to charge. Average range and invasive driver aids qualify a verdict judged very favourable for the price.
p: Fine equipment and build quality for the price
m: Average range for a long-distance car
No parcel shelf or front boot
XPeng|P7+.q: High-mileage drivers wanting a comfortable saloon that charges quickly
XPeng|P7+.s: Built in China then partly assembled at Magna Steyr in Austria, it does not qualify for the French eco-score. 7-year or 160,000 km warranty.
XPeng|P7+.x: The Long Range, the only version tested, adds nappa leather and ventilated, massaging rear seats; the Standard Range has a smaller battery that charges more slowly.
